There are [unclear]; all the rest perished in the inundation of the waters. The cause of their perishing was sin; but that they were created had no other cause than the uncircumscribed goodness of God. For few are saved while many perish. The figure preceded the mystery: Noah’s ark was the sacrament of the Christian faith. For just as all who were outside Noah’s ark perished in the flood, so now all who are outside the unity of the Catholic Church of Christians will without doubt perish eternally in their sins, Jews as well as pagans, heretics together with schismatics. The justice of God condemns those whom his goodness created. But mercy saves those whom grace has strengthened, because, as the holy Apostle says, it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy, since he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. Let us rightly weigh the freedom of human choice, and we shall know the just will of God.

On the Miracles of Unbelievers. The Third Question.

Your Most Serene Majesty’s third question was this: if no one is saved outside the faith, whence come miracles among unbelievers, since we know from the report of many that astonishing things are also done among unbelievers? As it seems to me, there will be no difficult solution to this question if we apply the necessary consideration to the faith of the Scriptures and to the natural powers of the soul.

A miracle is a new and unusual occurrence, which happens beyond custom and draws men into wonder. Hence good Christians, wicked Christians, and unbelievers perform miracles in different ways. Good Christians perform miracles through public righteousness; the wicked, through the signs of public righteousness; but unbelievers through private contracts with demons, whether implicit or explicit. Of the good the Lord said in the holy Gospel: “These signs shall follow those who have believed. In my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not harm them. They shall lay their hands upon the sick, and they shall be well.” But concerning wicked Christians who perform miracles in the name of Jesus Christ, we read thus written in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works? And then I will declare to them: I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity.”

But outside the Church of God, where the name of our Lord Jesus Christ is not invoked, if any wonders are done beyond the custom of nature or of human art, no good Christian doubts that they are done by the cooperation of demons. And Your Most Serene Caesarean Majesty, by discerning their power, judges that works of this sort should be called wonders rather than miracles. Nor does this judgment of truth depart from reason, so that a necessary distinction may be maintained between the prodigies of light and of darkness.

I find four effectors of wonders; but I acknowledge one alone, God, who truly performs miracles principally as the cause of all honors. Therefore the first and greatest effector of all wonderful things is God, who filled and illumined the whole world with signs, miracles, and powers. None of the others is to be compared with him, who created heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them; who alone is almighty, just, holy and upright, good, incomprehensible, greatest, glorious, immeasurable, and everlasting. All other things are beneath him, since whatever can happen wonderfully in this world is certainly less than the whole world itself, which he was able to create out of nothing.

Every miracle that can be done through man is less than man himself, whom God, the creator of all things, formed from the beginning in his image and likeness. And although the miracles of God in visible natures have now, through the frequency with which mortals see them, almost become cheapened, nevertheless, if we look upon them wisely, they will appear greater and rarer than all things that are unusual.

Now the manner in which God performs miracles is the immutable will of God, which, since it is omnipotent, does all things whatsoever it has willed in heaven and on earth. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. The will of God is ordered and eternal; therefore his miracles are incomparably greater than all others. For greater than the miracles of this whole world is what we perceive: the entire universe, and whatever is contained in it, created by the will of God. The immutable divine will works all things, abiding forever, since it lacks beginning and end; but whatever God wills, he always wills, because, since in him to will and to be able are the same, there is no labor for the immutable one. Hence all the universal miracles which [unclear].

12
18 quae conditor facit universorũ et bonis et ma- lis spectanda exhibuit, atque post generalia que iam usu uiluerunt apud mortales, in singulis pe ne creaturis infinita quoque specialiter miranda demonstrauit. Secundus miraculorũ effector bonus est angelus, qui miranda plerumque morta- libus tam uirtute naturali quam divina potesta te operatur. Mittuntur enim beatissimi illi spi ritus ordinatione diuina in ministerium fidelibus qui et bonis et malis ea que sunt naturae bene ficia praestât, solis autẽ credentibus in deum et dominum nostrum Iesum Christum dona gratia salutaris administrant. Vnde non est dubiũ ea miracula que fiunt inuocatione diuini nominis in ecclesia sanctoru, ministerio et cooperatione ipsoru exhiberi. Sed mirada infidelii si qua uel hodie fiũ uel olim facta leguntur, aut conficta aut emẽtita sunt, aut doemonũ ludificatiõe pa- trantur. Non enim fieri potest ut ministerio bo norum angelorum infideles quique miracula fa- ciant, quoniam ubi Christus Iesus Dei filius non creditur, nulla gratiae signa per bonos spi- ritus impiis et reprobis hominibus exhiben- tur. Eni:uero cum sint in errore falsae religiõis abstinati, si quid miraculi fuerint in sua aestimatione assecuti, per ministerium fieri daemonum nullatenus est dubitandum. Nam cum sint bonis angelis omnino dissimiles, nullam eorum assequuntur familiaritatem. Nullus aut cotemptor fidei Christianae Deo placere potest, sed quis quid omnipotenti Deo disiplere convincitur, familiaritate sanctorum angelorum proculdubio priuatitur. Per hoc tamen non retractamus omnem hominem boni alicui spiritui esse commissum, cuius ministerio etiam si sit incredulus dei filio, beneficia naturae suscipiat, quamuis ad dona gratiae non pertingat. His uero qui credunt in dominum nostrum Iesum Christum non solum naturae beneficia conferunt, etiam gratiae munera ministrant. Manifestũ est ergo quod si qua fiunt apud infideles miracula, non Dei munere, neque sanctorum ministerio angelorum fieri poterũt, cum extra unitatem Ecclesie omnes sint positi, signa per iusticiam publicam ab impiis neque ant operari. Deus enim sicut dictum est iram suam originalem ab homine no remouet nisi per fidem Iefu Christi, sed omnis qui incredulus est Dei filio, non uidebit uitam aeternam, sed ira dei manet 19 mdnet super eum. Omnis ergo super quem ma- net ira Dei Deo placere non poterit, & ideò si qua ad eius preces fiunt miranda, non Dei uirtu- te nec angelorum ministerio, sed doemonum po- tius suppositione credantur acclitata. Tertius mirandorum effector est diabolus, qui quasi simia imitari gliscit quodcunque vide- rit, & mentes hominum maximè infidelium ua- rijs illusionibus decipit et sibi credentes quadam miraculorum similitudine seducit. Neque enim difficile iudico doemonibus sensus ludificare pos- se hominum, quos constat natura cunctis morta- libus conditos subtiliores. Scire autem cogitaz- tiones mortalium nisi coniectura quadam non possunt: cum uidelicet interiora nostra quibus- dam signis facimus manifesta. Doemones futura praenunciant, et aliquando vera dicunt, aliquando decipiuntur coniecturantes, & fallunt. Ab ini- tio mundi rem antecedentia quaedam signa no- uerunt, quorum experientia et usu, uerum quod futurum est nonnunquam praenunciât, quoniam cum nota sibi rem praecedentia signa uiderint, statim quid in cogitatione sit hominis coiiciunt. C. 3 Sapius tamen fallunt, quoniam falluntur ipsi. Cum enim de aliquo interrogantur nego cio quod nesciunt: quemadmodum si nuncius pro cul emissus cito, vel quo die sit reversurus, statim in ielu oculi perueniunt in eum locum ubi illum esse nouerunt, quem cum uiderint iam inchoasse iter ad reuertendum dietas studiose numerant, et subito reversi ad interrogantem, certo absentem die confirmant esse uenturum. Quia si ille aut moram in via traxerit, aut aliorum declinauerit, certe daemones, iudicio suo deceptos iam necesse est falli. Libenter se uaticinjs immiscent, et satvs promptuli sunt ad praedicendum futura hominibus honoris et aestimationis gratia, quoniam haberi admiratioe digni maxime cupiunt, honores divinos appetunt, et timeri a mortalibus ualde concupiscunt. Quemadmodum pueri in abdito latitantes aut discurretes laruati subito erumpentes de latibulis suis coe uos nil tale suspicatex ex inopinato terrore concutiunt, et rursus ne cognoscantur se iterum ab scondunt, qui cum nescientes territos consyderant quasi magnum ex hoc uideantur assecuti hono

which the Creator of all things has made and has displayed for both good and evil men to behold; and, after the general wonders that have now grown cheap by use among mortals, he has also shown, in almost every single creature, infinite things specially worthy of wonder.

The second worker of miracles is a good angel, who very often works wonders for mortals both by natural power and by divine authority. For those most blessed spirits are sent, by divine ordination, into ministry for the faithful; and they bestow upon both good and evil men those things that are benefits of nature, but only to those who believe in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ do they administer the gifts of saving grace. Hence there is no doubt that those miracles which are done in the Church of the saints by invocation of the divine name are displayed through their ministry and cooperation. But the wonders of unbelievers, if any are done today or are read to have been done in former times, are either fabricated or falsely invented, or are performed by the mockery of demons. For it cannot be that any unbelievers work miracles through the ministry of good angels, since where Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is not believed in, no signs of grace are displayed by good spirits to impious and reprobate men. Indeed, since they are obstinate in the error of false religion, if they have attained anything miraculous in their own estimation, it must in no way be doubted that it is done through the ministry of demons. For since they are altogether unlike the good angels, they attain no familiarity with them.

No despiser of the Christian faith can please God; but whoever is proved to displease almighty God is without doubt deprived of the fellowship of the holy angels. Yet by this we do not retract the point that every man is committed to some good spirit, by whose ministry, even if he is an unbeliever in the Son of God, he may receive the benefits of nature, although he does not attain to the gifts of grace. But to those who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ they not only confer the benefits of nature, but also minister the gifts of grace. It is therefore clear that if any miracles are done among unbelievers, they cannot be done by the gift of God or by the ministry of the holy angels, since all such people are placed outside the unity of the Church, and signs cannot be worked by the impious through public righteousness. For God, as has been said, does not remove his original wrath from man except through faith in Jesus Christ; but everyone who is unbelieving toward the Son of God will not see eternal life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore everyone upon whom the wrath of God remains cannot please God; and for that reason, if any wonders are done at his prayers, they should be believed to have been accomplished not by the power of God nor by the ministry of angels, but rather by the substitution of demons.

The third worker of wonders is the devil, who, like an ape, longs to imitate whatever he has seen, and deceives the minds of men, especially unbelievers, with various illusions, and seduces those who believe him by a certain likeness of miracles. For I do not judge it difficult for demons to be able to mock the senses of men, since it is agreed that by nature they were created more subtle than all mortals. But they cannot know the thoughts of mortals except by a certain conjecture, namely when we make our inner thoughts manifest by certain signs. Demons foretell future things, and sometimes they speak truth, while sometimes they are deceived in their conjectures and deceive others. From the beginning of the world they have known certain signs that precede events; by experience and practice with these, they sometimes foretell the truth about what is going to happen, because when they have seen signs known to them that precede an event, they at once conjecture what is in a man’s thought.

Yet more often they deceive, because they themselves are deceived. For when they are asked about some matter that they do not know, for example whether a messenger sent far away will return soon, or on what day, they immediately arrive in the blink of an eye at the place where they know him to be; and when they see that he has already begun his journey back, they carefully count the days’ stages, and, returning at once to the one who asked, confidently affirm the day on which the absent man will come. But if he has either delayed on the road or turned aside to other places, then certainly the demons, deceived in their judgment, must now be mistaken. They gladly involve themselves in prophecies, and are quite ready to predict future things to men for the sake of honor and esteem, because they especially desire to be regarded as worthy of admiration, they seek divine honors, and they greatly desire to be feared by mortals. Just as boys hiding in secret places, or running about masked, suddenly burst out from their hiding places and shake their companions, who suspect nothing of the sort, with unexpected terror, and then hide themselves again so that they may not be recognized; when they see the ignorant ones terrified, they seem to themselves to have gained from this some great honor.

13
bonorem gloriantur. Horum daemones quidam exempla terrae magis affixi, & qui circa homines versantur nimis inquieti, quos ueteres ap- pellauere bacuccos homines, noctibus territant, et nihil magis quà aestimatione divinitatis à mor- talibus quaerunt. Vnde et coram his cum quibus ratione similitudinis esse permittuntur uarias lu- dificationes nonnunquã faciunt, & se terribiles in mentibus pro ut casus dederit offerunt. Quo- tiens possunt humani similitudinem corporis li- benter induunt, scd non semper conuenientem aëris materiam unde uestiantur inueniunt. Pro- pterea soepius apparet mōstruos et horribiles, quoniam congruos uel humores uel uapores ad perfectionem optatae apparetae non habuerūt. Quanto autem magis terrenis affixi sunt manfi onibus, tanto ex casu ad materiae facti sunt obtu fiores. Vnde propter ignorantiam, qua inobedi- entia contraxerunt, praedictiones daemoni fre- quenter sunt falsae, licet diuina permissione ali quando etiam uerificentur. Nam ut sanctissimus ille Ioannes Chrysostomus inquit: Concessum est diabolo interdum ueritatem dicere, ut mendac- cium suũ rara ueritate commédet, quia si nunq dicet verum, neminem posset decipere, & ne quaquam ad tentandum sufficeret eius sedu- ctio. Mirandum igitur non est si daemones homi- nibus infidelibus aliquando vera videantur pra- dicere, qui uaticinia in idolis quondam gentili- bus poterant exhibere. Neque mirandum si curam quandoque praetet infirmantibus, cum naturas no- uerint omnium herbarum, seque facilime applica- re possint aegrotis, & uel auferre morbos quos prius intulerunt, uel sensibus ad tempus subtra- here quos casus inflixit. Vititur enim omnip- tens Deus iure imperatoriae maiestatis univer- sorum, etiam daemonum ministerio tam ad pro- bationem fidelium quam ad vindictam impio- rum. Qui cum sint affectione peruersi et in sua rebellione obstinati atque superbi, divinas aesti- mationes et honores maxime cupiunt, & pro- pterea invocationibus infidelium quas ad deos suos effundere solent, quasi ipsi sint dii libenter occurrunt. Mortuos quandoque apud infideles re- fuscitare uidentur ad uitam, & curiosis homini- bus miranda ostendunt, ut eos in errore pristi- no quasi miraculis consumatos reddant omnino pertinaces. Mortuos tamen vere non refuscitant, sed 21 Sed hominum sensus varie decipiunt, quoniam quidem aut ipsi cadavera mortuorum ingressi ad tempus illa circumferunt tanquam uiva, aut illis in locum remotiorem subductis, aliquod in specie uita defuncti simulachrum intuentibus ex- hibent uidendum, sicut nos quorundam experien- tia hominum informauit. Manifestum credimus daemones omnia posse ostendere in falsa quaedam similitudine, quaecuj; sancti faciunt mira- cula in ueritate. Omnia daemoni miracula aut sunt fantasmata, aut naturali quaeda industria facta. Nam si homines in occultioribus naturae mysterijs experti, quaedam obstrusa caeteris ap- plicatione materia ad formam imconsuetos et mirandos producunt effectus, sicuti ex rore coeli naturales formare anguillas, ex uitulinis carni- bus apes, ex quibusdam radicibus herbarum ser- pentes, et his multa similia ne dicam maiorda. Sicut nos in plaerisque probatio fecit expertos, quis neget daemones subtilioris naturae et ma- ioris experientiae plura posse operari naturali- ter miranda, quae nulli hominu sunt manifesta. Quartus uero miraculorum operator est ho- mo, qui quatuor modis operatur miranda, que nescientibus uel causam uel modum non uidentur humana. Et primo quidem invocatione divini nominis, quando in fide domini nostri Iesu Christi concurrit meritum accepte sanctitatis. Quo quidem modo sancti apostoli et imitatores eorum, virtute Dei simul et merito sanctitatis in unitate fidei miracula fecerunt. Sed isto modo facere miracula infideles nequeunt, qui ne cessarium iter fidei ad salutem non incedunt. Nam si unum plerique credunt in deum quia tamem credere in mediatori deo hominu renuunt, a dei misericordia procul malde exces ferunt. Omnia uero promittente sancto Evangelio credentibus in deum dominum nostrum Iesum Christum sunt possibilia, his uidelicet qui fidem rectam sanctis quod decorant operibus. Enimuero quemadmodum sine fide impossibile est placere deo, ita etiam fides sine operibus mortua est. Omnia namque concederet nobis omnipotens Deus que in fide Christi petimus, si faceremus omnia secundum fidem quae debemus. Crede firmiter et operare fideliter, et impretrabis omnia semper. Secundo facit miracula homo similitudine angelicae

Some demons of these, more fastened to the earthly elements and, because they go about among men, exceedingly restless, whom the ancients called bacucci, terrify men by night, and seek nothing more from mortals than to be thought divine. Hence, in the presence of those with whom they are permitted to be by reason of likeness, they sometimes perform various mockeries, and present themselves in men’s minds as terrifying, as occasion allows.

Whenever they can, they gladly put on the likeness of a human body, but they do not always find a suitable material of air with which to clothe themselves. Therefore they more often appear monstrous and horrible, because they have not had suitable fluids or vapors for the perfection of the desired appearance. And the more they are fastened to earthly dwellings, the duller they have become through their fall in regard to matter. Hence, because of the ignorance which they contracted through disobedience, the predictions of demons are frequently false, although by divine permission they are sometimes also verified. For, as that most holy John Chrysostom says, the devil is sometimes allowed to speak the truth, so that he may commend his lie by a rare truth; for if he never spoke truth, he could deceive no one, and his seduction would by no means suffice for temptation.

It is therefore no wonder if demons sometimes seem to foretell true things to unbelieving men, since they were once able to furnish prophecies among the idols of the Gentiles. Nor is it any wonder if they sometimes show care for the sick, since they know the natures of all herbs, can most easily apply themselves to the diseased, and can either remove illnesses which they had previously inflicted, or for a time withdraw from the senses those which accident has brought on. For almighty God, by the right of imperial majesty over all things, uses even the ministry of demons, both for the testing of the faithful and for the punishment of the impious.

Since they are perverse in affection, obstinate in their rebellion, and proud, they very greatly desire to be regarded and honored as divine; and therefore, when unbelievers pour out invocations to their gods, as they are accustomed to do, the demons gladly come to them as though they themselves were gods. Among unbelievers they sometimes seem to restore the dead to life, and they show marvelous things to curious men, so that, as though confirmed by miracles in their former error, they may become utterly obstinate. Yet they do not truly restore the dead, but deceive men’s senses in various ways: either they themselves enter the corpses of the dead and carry them about for a time as though alive, or, after the bodies have been removed to a more distant place, they present to the beholders some image in the likeness of the deceased person’s life, as the experience of certain men has taught us.

We believe it manifest that demons can show, in a certain false likeness, all the things that the saints perform as miracles in truth. All demonic miracles are either phantasms or works produced by a certain natural skill. For if men experienced in the more hidden mysteries of nature, by applying matter to form in ways obscure to others, produce unusual and marvelous effects, such as forming natural eels from the dew of heaven, bees from calves’ flesh, serpents from certain roots of herbs, and many things like these, not to mention greater ones, as trial has made us experienced in very many cases, who will deny that demons, being of subtler nature and greater experience, can naturally perform many marvelous things which are manifest to no men?

The fourth worker of miracles is man, who works marvels in four ways, which to those who know neither their cause nor their manner do not seem human. First, by invocation of the divine name, when, in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merit of accepted holiness concurs. In this way the holy apostles and their imitators performed miracles by the power of God, together with the merit of holiness, in the unity of faith. But unbelievers cannot perform miracles in this way, since they do not walk the necessary path of faith toward salvation. For although many believe in one God, yet because they refuse to believe in the mediator between God and men, they have gone far away from God’s mercy. But, by the promise of the holy Gospel, all things are possible to those who believe in God, our Lord Jesus Christ, namely to those who adorn right faith with holy works. For just as without faith it is impossible to please God, so also faith without works is dead. For almighty God would grant us all things that we ask in the faith of Christ, if we did all things according to the faith as we ought. Believe firmly and work faithfully, and you will always obtain all things.

Secondly, man performs miracles by likeness of angelic [unclear].

14
licae puritatis. Quando enim mens nostra in fide Iesu Christi confirmata per dilectionem purior euaserit, tanto sanctis angelis effecta similior, eorum familiaritate maiorem assequitur. Quis quis autem sanctorum angelorum omnimodum familiaritatem assecutus fuerit, cum uoluerit in miraculis Deo largiente choruscabit. Reue- lant enim sancti angeli hominib. puris et in dei amore feruentibus archana caeteris abscondita, & multa faciunt eis mandato creatoris manife- sta. Nam prope est dominus inuocantibus eum in ueritate. Voluntate timentiũ se faciet dominus, et deprecationes eorũ exaudiet, et saluos faciet eos. Quisquis enim per gratiã cu Christo uni- cusest, angelorum crebra uisitatione reficitur, & sepius cum necessitas expostulat eorum mis- nisterio signis et virtutibus illustratur. Hinc est quod etiam uarijs depressi languoribus ad suffragia sanctorum se conferunt, & promissa domini reuoluentes animo quod suis meritis ne queũt alienis consequũtur. Quoru in fide Chri sti sancta deuotio salutẽ domini pcipit, quonia et puritate adiuta cõsciẽtiae propriae et suffulta merito sanctitatis alienae in spẽ certã no temere consurgit. Fiunt autem in Ecclesia dei miracula virtute divina triplici respectu vel medio. Ali- quando nang Deus omnipotens miraculum ope ratur ministerio angelorum, meritis duntaxat ipsius operantis, quemadmodum Sanctus Marti- nus coecum et claudum sanavit inuitos. Ali- quando solius merito patientis fiunt miracula, si cuti plures curatos legimus per malos Christia- nos, quos infirmi optimos in fide crediderunt. Tertio huiusmodi sanitatos fieri utriusque me- rito pacientis uidelicet simul et operantis non est dubitandum, Christo dicente ad quandam in Sancto Evangelio: Si potes credere, omnia possi bilia sunt credenti. Vsque enim fides requiritur ad miraculum, ut dominus noster Iesus Christus veniens in patriam suam miraretur quod non poterat ibi facere uirtutem ullam propter incre- dulitatem illorum. Sed nihil horum apud infide- les agitur, ubi nec in operatione sanctitas, nec in patiente fides orthodoxa inuenitur. Tertio igitur miracula facit homo median- te cooperatione diabolica prauitatis, & hoc fie- ri potest tripliciter manifesta uidelicet in inuoc- atione daemonum, implicatione et suppositio- ne. 23 Ne Invocatione manifesta necromantici et mulierculae quas vulgo maleficas nuncupamus miranda faciunt, qui similitudine voluntatis depravati in consortium daemonum transierunt. Nam sic ut in Ecclesia Dei sacramenta signa sunt gratie invisibilis spiritus sancti, ita in schola daemoniorum characteres quidam et invocationis modi notae sunt pacti hominis et spiritus maligni. Unde malefici daemonum signa preferentibus maligni spiritus inuocati libenter consueuerunt occurrere, & horreda maleficia simul et miranda quaedam exhibere. Sed aliter malefica atque aliter necromantici daemonum invocatione mirandos producunt effectus. Malefica quodam professionis genere subiiciuntur daemonibus, quorum ministerio aerem turbant, tempestates iuscitant, fruges deuastant, homines et iumenta infirmant, agunt cum daemonibus spurcisime uoluptatis foeda commertia, & eos pernitiosis carminibus quos uoluerint ab inferis reuocant in aspectum. Harum facta non miracula sed pauius maleficia dicenda sunt, & extremo suplicio merito punienda. Necromantici uero non professione manifesta, sed implicita conditione de monibus se subjiciunt, dum eos non solum coniurationibus et ostensione characterum, sed etiam sacrificis fumigis et votis ad circulum uisibiles compellere pollicentur. Horum infinitas sunt sceleras, quoniam in consortium daemonum uel implicite uel explicite omnes conspirare manifestum est. Quamuis autem necromantici non omnes uel arte uel opere sint pares, in perniciem tamen propriam damnabili curiositate omnes sunt concordes, qua daemoni suffragio cupiunt ussequi, quod naturaliter nequeunt inuenire. Omnia eorum et opera et uolumina superstitionibus et impietate sunt plena, & ob id procul à finibus credentiũ exterminanda. Magna incantatorum et necromanticorum in oriente multitudo est, qui suis praestigiis humanum genus miserabiliter decipiunt, & pene totam Asyam maiorem et minorem à fide Christi auerterunt. Tribus modis fieri praestigia possunt ministerio daemonum, operatione naturae et deceptione artis humane. Miracula infidelium uno istorum fieri modo nullus duabit uerus christianorum, ubi radix ponitur determinata operantis. Sunt autem hodie com=

For when our mind, confirmed in the faith of Jesus Christ, has become purer through love, then, having been made more like the holy angels, it obtains greater intimacy with them. And whoever has obtained complete intimacy with the holy angels will, whenever he wishes, shine forth in miracles, God granting it. For the holy angels reveal to pure men, fervent in the love of God, secrets hidden from others, and by command of the Creator they make many things manifest to them. For the Lord is near to those who call upon him in truth. The Lord will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers and save them. For whoever by grace is one with Christ is refreshed by frequent visitation of the angels, and often, when necessity demands it, is made illustrious by signs and powers through their ministry. Hence it is that even those weighed down by various illnesses betake themselves to the intercessions of the saints, and, turning over in their mind the promises of the Lord, obtain through the merits of others what they cannot obtain by their own. Their holy devotion in the faith of Christ receives the Lord’s salvation, because, aided by the purity of their own conscience and supported by the merit of another’s holiness, it rises, not rashly, into certain hope.

Miracles are done in the Church of God by divine power with a threefold respect or means. Sometimes almighty God works a miracle through the ministry of angels, solely by the merits of the one who performs it, as Saint Martin healed the blind man and the lame man against their will. Sometimes miracles are done solely by the merit of the sufferer, as we read that many were cured through bad Christians whom the sick believed to be very good in the faith. Third, there is no doubt that healings of this kind are done by the merit of both, that is, of the sufferer and the one performing it together, as Christ says to a certain person in the holy Gospel: If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes. For faith is required for a miracle to such a degree that our Lord Jesus Christ, coming into his own country, marveled that he could do no mighty work there because of their unbelief. But none of these things is done among unbelievers, where neither holiness in the working nor orthodox faith in the sufferer is found.

Third, then, a man performs miracles through the mediation of the cooperation of diabolical wickedness, and this can happen in three ways: namely by manifest invocation of demons, by involvement, and by supposition.

By manifest invocation, necromancers and the little women whom we commonly call witches do wondrous things, who, corrupted by a likeness of will, have passed into fellowship with demons. For just as in the Church of God the sacraments are signs of the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, so in the school of demons certain characters and modes of invocation are marks of the pact between man and the malignant spirit. Hence, when witches display the signs of demons, the malignant spirits invoked are accustomed gladly to appear, and to produce both horrible acts of witchcraft and certain wondrous things.

But witches and necromancers produce wondrous effects by the invocation of demons in different ways. Witches subject themselves to demons by a certain kind of profession; by their ministry they disturb the air, raise storms, lay waste crops, make men and beasts sick, carry on foul commerce of most filthy lust with demons, and by destructive spells call back from the underworld into sight whomever they wish. Their deeds are not to be called miracles, but rather acts of witchcraft, and they deservedly are to be punished with the utmost penalty.

Necromancers, however, subject themselves to demons not by manifest profession but by an implicit condition, when they claim that they can compel them visibly to the circle not only by conjurations and the display of characters, but also by sacrifices, fumigations, and vows. Their crimes are countless, since it is plain that all of them conspire in fellowship with demons, either implicitly or explicitly. Although necromancers are not all equal either in art or in practice, nevertheless all are agreed, to their own destruction, in damnable curiosity, by which they desire to obtain by demonic aid what they cannot discover naturally. All their works and books are full of superstitions and impiety, and for that reason they must be driven far from the borders of believers.

There is a great multitude of enchanters and necromancers in the East, who by their illusions miserably deceive the human race, and have turned almost all Greater and Lesser Asia away from the faith of Christ. Illusions can be produced in three ways: by the ministry of demons, by the operation of nature, and by the deception of human art. No true Christian will doubt that the miracles of unbelievers are done in one of these ways, where the root of the operator is determined. There are today [unclear].

24 complures inter Christianos daemonum operibus dediti, incantatores, malefici, & reprobi circa fidem, qui multos nimia curiositate decipiunt, & suis artibus impossibilia promittunt. There are many among Christians, devoted to the works of demons: enchanters, sorcerers, and those reprobate concerning the faith, who deceive many by excessive curiosity and by their arts promise impossible things.

By the involvement of demons, however, marvels sometimes occur, namely whenever a person not sufficiently and rightly established in the faith does or desires something otherwise than befits a Christian, even if he does not believe it to be any sin; and although it ought not to happen, nevertheless the devil, inserting himself, often supplies the desired effect. Such, indeed, is what sufferers from spasms commonly use. On the holy day of Good Friday they fashion a ring of whatever metal during the office, which afterward they always wear on the ring finger. These things are utterly vain and have no root of truth at all. Yet I cannot deny that I have seen certain people cured by this same vanity and freed from spasm.

Likewise, I know that certain people have opened very strong locks with words and herbs, which I do not think was done either by the power of God or by the force of the things applied. I could introduce countless similar things that I have seen and heard; what are their manifest effects other than certain miracles of demons?

Finally, there are some excessively curious people who stubbornly put faith and confidence in characters, slips of paper, rings, figures, necklaces, and unknown words, and often obtain marvelous effects; we in no way doubt that the devil has supplied these, not by merit of holiness nor by God’s merciful concession, but rather through faithless credulity. For demons, having the greatest envy of the human race, in order to destroy the souls of mortals, gladly come to meet the vain operations of the impious. What else are characters and interpretations of hidden names but certain foods and drinks of demons? Whoever puts faith in characters promising marvelous effects has implicitly denied the faith of Christ and the Church of the saints. Alas, how many Christians today, how many clerics, how many priests, to say nothing of greater persons, use many and various superstitions in their daily actions, by which they follow pacts with demons entangled in them, to the disgrace of the Christian faith and their own condemnation. And because these evils have now multiplied far too much among Christians, the Almighty has withdrawn his hand and delivered them into the dominion of the faithless, so that they may feel as exactors of punishments those whose example they followed when they stubbornly served not the living and true God, but vain superstitions.

Moreover, if we inquire more diligently into the truth, we plainly recognize that marvels are done by the substitution of demons. For if Jews, Saracens, pagans, or gentiles, who do not believe in our God, Jesus Christ, perform any miracles, we believe they are done not by the power of God, not by the ministry of angels, not by the merit of holiness, but through the substitution of demons. For as often as they invoke almighty God, in whose only-begotten Son they do not believe, for the mercy of some marvelous effect, the devil, knowing that there is no salvation for sinners and that the Most High does not hear unbelieving sinners, secretly applies himself in place of the God invoked, in order to preserve them stubborn in their errors; and if he can, with the Lord permitting it, he grants to those praying what is requested. The devil uses this substitution all the more freely, the less he is hindered by faith in Christ and the sacraments of the Church. For the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers who do not believe in his only-begotten Son, and they are in the power of the devil; and therefore he thrusts himself upon those who invoke him, in place of God.

Thus, blinded in their errors, they invoke God, in whose Son they do not believe; and since he despises hearing them while they remain under wrath, the devil, the false worker of miracles, approaches. Therefore those who scorn believing the true miracles of God believe the mockeries of the devil. Those who refused by believing to follow the truth, that is, Christ, receive from demons false miracles suited to their errors.

For there are many among unbelievers who worship one God, creator of all things, do not adore idols, and firmly believe that they will be saved in their own faith. But because they scorn believing the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the wrath of God remains upon them, and they vanish away in their foolishness. Thinking God to be near to them, though they do not believe rightly in him, they are subjected to demons; and by putting faith in their false miracles, they are confirmed in their errors by a lie. It is not irksome, O Caesar, to introduce a likeness of this matter.

Con tigit pertransire uidentem absente pastore qui cernens daemonem custodiam habere gregis, di xit ad eum. Quid miser hic agis? Qui respondit istos custodio porcos. At ille. Verum quia inuocatus non comparet, ego ne homo confidentia suam amitteret porcos eius custodio, & me pro Blasio libens suppono. Ita inquit mortales uanis coniurationibus nos molestant, ut nisi uelimus aestimationem nostri et honorem apud eos perdere omnem, necesse sit eorum inuocationibus stultis plerumque occur- ramus. Huius similitudine facti daemones miseri cordes infideles decipiunt, et miracula que oran- tes a deo postulant malignorum spirituum sup- D 2 positione soepius sessequuntur. In his enim que Dei vel cultum respiciunt vel honorẽ libenter se daemones ingerunt, & qui manifestos honores assequi nequunt, occultis nimirum delesantur. Simul notandum quod ab initio mundi, nulli un quam religioni vel secte principaliter excellen ti defuere miracula, quamuis non omnia ex uno principio sint facta. Nam quicquid miraculo rum in vera religione factum est, non aliunde quam à Deo factum est. Habuit enim lex naturae miracula sua, habuit lex scripta, habet iam si mul et gratia. Qui religionẽ dedit omnipotens Deus, ipse etiam miracula facit. In falsis autem religionibus ubi ueritas non colitur, si qua fiunt miracula non Deus sed diabolus operatur. Deus enim cum sit ueritas religiones falsas non instituit, & ideo suis miraculis nunquam men dacium illustrauit. Mahumet qui malo daemon plenus falsam religionem instituit, non ex Deo sed cooperatione daemonum falsis eam miracu lis exornauit. Daemon etenim qui causam dedit erroris, etiam miraculum (occasione tamem ac cepta) falsum potuit exhibere deceptis. Vnde si Mahumeto nouam religionem rudi populo per suadenti Suadenti penitus defuissent miracula, nemo ei forsitan adhibuisset fidem. Ostendit enim et ipse tam subtilitate ingenii quam cooperatione diaboli quaedam miranda populis, ut nouam do- stinam novis quoque miraculis confirmasse uide retur. Paganis idolatris etiam non defuerunt mi- racula, si fidem historijs non negamus. Iudaei vero ante incarnationem filij Dei legem eius fuscipientes per Mosen divinis frequentem mir- aculis fuerunt illustrati. At vero post dominica resurrectionem euacuata lege Mosaica qui non credunt in unigenitum filium Dei manet sub ira indignationis eius, et cessauerunt ab eis omnia miracula ueritatis. Unde si qua hodie mirada fa- ciunt daemonum sunt opera, et manifesta iudic- cia erroris. Maximo enim daemones studio inui- gilant ut eos homines quos via ueritatis que Christus est semel fecerunt errantes, continua- tione fraudis usque ad mortem faciant in errore pertinaces. Enim uero Deus gratiam suam in fidelibus iustaratione subtrahit, eorum decep- tor malignus spiritus incognitus accedit, et qui longe salutem abesse confpicit, falsis miraculis quasi propè sit dominus mentes ignorantium se- D 3 ducit. Daemnum igitur sunt opera quaecunque in fidelium miracula, quoniam sicut extra unitatem Christianae fidei non est salus mortalibus, ita sine Christo non conceditur mirabilium sanctissima virtus. Nunc etenim daemones et insidijs latitantes trophaeo Christi dudum uicti atque confusi, in aperto comparere ut ante incarnationem dominii metuunt, et ideo se apud infideles pro bonis spiritibus mendaciter ostendunt.

...he would believe every wolf barred from approach. With this foolish confidence at last strengthened by long experience, the man went safely wherever he wished, leaving his pigs in the wood without danger, since no wolf any longer had access to them.

It happened that someone passing by saw, while the swineherd was absent, that a demon had charge of the herd, and said to him, “What are you doing here, wretch?” He answered, “I am guarding those pigs.” The other said, “Who entrusted the care of the pigs to you?” Again he answered, “The foolish confidence of the swineherd. For he has sinned against his own law and follows our vanities, believing that a certain slip of paper enclosed in a staff is of great holy power, by which, through the merits of a certain Blasius, wolves are kept away from the pigs. But because Blasius, though invoked, does not appear, I guard the man’s pigs so that he may not lose his confidence, and I willingly put myself in place of Blasius. In this way,” he said, “mortals trouble us with vain conjurations, so that, unless we are willing to lose all esteem and honor among them, we must very often answer their foolish invocations.”

By the likeness of this deed, demons in seeming mercy deceive unbelievers, and the miracles which those who pray ask from God very often follow through the substitution of malignant spirits. For in matters that concern either the worship or the honor of God, demons gladly thrust themselves in; and those who cannot obtain open honors are, of course, delighted by hidden ones.

At the same time it must be noted that, from the beginning of the world, no religion or sect of outstanding principal rank has ever lacked miracles, although they have not all been done from one source. For whatever miracles have been done in the true religion have been done from no other source than God. The law of nature had its miracles; the written law had them; and now grace too has them. The almighty God who gave religion also performs miracles. But in false religions, where truth is not worshiped, if any miracles are done, it is not God but the devil who works them.

For God, since he is truth, did not establish false religions, and therefore he never adorned a lie with his miracles. Muhammad, who, filled with an evil demon, established a false religion, adorned it with false miracles not from God but by the cooperation of demons. For the demon who gave the cause of error could also, once an occasion had been taken, display a false miracle to those deceived. Hence, if miracles had been entirely lacking to Muhammad when he was persuading an untaught people to accept a new religion, perhaps no one would have believed him. For he too, both by subtlety of intellect and by the cooperation of the devil, showed certain marvels to the peoples, so that he might seem to have confirmed a new doctrine also with new miracles. Pagan idolaters too did not lack miracles, if we do not deny credit to the histories.

The Jews, however, before the incarnation of the Son of God, receiving his law through Moses, were frequently illumined by divine miracles. But after the Lord’s resurrection, when the Mosaic law had been made void, whoever do not believe in the only-begotten Son of God remain under the wrath of his indignation, and all miracles of truth have ceased among them. Hence, if they do any marvels today, they are works of demons and manifest judgments of error. For demons keep watch with the greatest zeal so that those men whom they have once made wander from the way of truth, which is Christ, they may, by the continuance of fraud, make obstinate in error until death. Indeed, when God for a just reason withdraws his grace from unbelievers, their deceiver, the malignant spirit, approaches unknown; and since he sees that salvation is far away, by false miracles he leads ignorant minds astray as if the Lord were near.

Therefore whatever miracles occur among unbelievers are works of demons, since just as there is no salvation for mortals outside the unity of the Christian faith, so without Christ the most holy power of wonders is not granted. For now demons, lurking in their snares, long ago conquered and confounded by the trophy of Christ, fear to appear openly as they did before the incarnation of the Lord; and therefore among unbelievers they falsely present themselves as good spirits.

Sunt etiam qui praescriptis tribus aduciit modis quartum, dicentes mentem siue spiritum ipsius hominis posse naturaliter miranda facere, modo sciat se ab omni aduentitio in seipsam supra sensum in unitatem revocare. Pollicentur enim qui talia astruunt naturae miranda facere, futura praedicere, secretas hominum pandere, morbos auferre, et hominum subito censilia imputare. Sed iste miraculorum modus non potest esse simpliciter naturalis, certus, communis et infallibilis, quoniam si uerus est quod ego non sum expertus, necesse est iam aliquid externae potestatis ocurrere, et uel angelum bonum uel spiritum malignum cogitantem in parte occupare. Si autem nihil exterarum virtutum se intermixet, 28 cet necesse est uaticinantem uel ex coniecturis uel ex audaci praesumptione loquendi formare principium, & aliquando uerum aliquando fal- sum pronunciare iudicium. Enimuero quam diu uersatur in corpore spiritus, nihil naturaliter intelligit sine ministerio sensus. Vnde non obni- terer penitus si confusum et rudem intellectum nostrum pari concedant ministerio adiuvari. Cernimus enim in his qui plerumque amoris inter ni ad Iesum desiderio carnis modum contem- plantes excedunt, à terra sursum leuatos in aera, quos non sua duntaxat acie mentis, sed di uina nihilominus uirtute pondus excedere cor- porale putamus. Tria igitur memoratae opinio- nis principia incognita multis, satis faciunt mea sententia paucis, ut mens in corpore posita mi- randos extra se propria uirtute operetur esse. Quid enim? Dicat mihi naturae quisquis igna- rurus, utrum corporale pondus operatione men- tis alleuiari possit. Ego contestantibus me- cum duobus, rem dico expertam. Cum proseque- rer adolescens studia literarum, in uno lecto quatuor eramus nocte quadam dormientes. Ascendit muros, & elucrum agilitate sua uince bat. Lectum quoque secundo et tertio sopitus tran scendit, calcauit nos pedibus omnes, nec maius sensimus pondus, quam simus nos contigisset exi guus. Quocunque dormiens corpus mouebatur, subito ianuarum omnes ultro aperiebantur clau surae. Altiora domus aedificia uel ocissimè pene= trauit, & more passeris haercbat in tectis. Visa loquor, non uaga relatione audita. Haec animae non corporis uidentur officia, quae sua naturali potestate ut ita dixerim, quasi liberè utitur, quando ligatis sensibus carnis extra domicilium corporis euagatur. Sed cum non sit propositae quaestioni materia ex omni parte conueniens, de causis horum mirabilium in aliud tempus re mittamus tractatum. Haud enim credimus ista miranda sapientibus qui mentis humanae uirtu= tem et nobilitatem optime intellexerunt, utpote quae solo corporis interieictu remorata, de relia quo par angelis aestimatur. Fascinationum deni que et uarios modos pertransimus et genera, quibus ad externa furiosus ualde mirandos ope 29 ratur effectus. Multa etiam potest ad producendos mirabiles effectus fortissime confidetis imaginatio, siue in verum, siue in aestimatum feratur obiectum. Unde cum tot sint operandi miranda genera et modi, non est mirandum, si Iudaei, Sarraconi, pagani, gentiles, ac reliqui extra fidem Christi constituti, quicunque infideles qui facere miracula per publicam iusticiamnequeunt, miranda uel doemenum suffragio uel artificiosa industria committunt. Nec me fugit pariet quidem ratione miracula sanctorum impugnari ab impiis quasi non uirtute creatoris sint sed potius implicatione uel suppositione diaboli. Quisquis Christianam fidem solam ueraciter credit esse ueram, omnium infidelium miracula cooperatione doemonum non dubitat esse patra ta. Si quis uero contrarium temere et pertinaciter senserit, infidelem se non Christianum ostendit. De scriptura Sacra Quaestio Quarta. Q varia uero serenissimae maiestatis tuae quaestio fuit ista. Quare omnipotens Deus scripturam sanctam tam noui

There are also those who add a fourth mode to the three already described, saying that the mind or spirit of the human being himself can naturally do marvelous things, provided it knows how to recall itself, away from everything adventitious, above sense, into unity within itself. For those who maintain such things promise that they can do marvels of nature, predict the future, disclose people’s secrets, remove diseases, and suddenly impress counsels upon human beings. But this mode of miracles cannot be simply natural, certain, common, and infallible; for if it is true, which I have not experienced, some external power must already be involved, and either a good angel or an evil spirit must occupy part of the one who is thinking. But if no power from outside mixes itself in, then it is necessary that the one prophesying form the beginning of his speech either from conjectures or from a bold presumption, and pronounce a judgment sometimes true and sometimes false.

For as long as the spirit dwells in the body, it naturally understands nothing without the service of sense. Hence I would not wholly resist if they grant that our confused and crude understanding is aided by a like service. For we see in those who, often in the desire of inward love for Jesus, through contemplation exceed the measure of the flesh, that they are lifted up from the earth into the air; and we think that they overcome bodily weight not only by their own keenness of mind, but also by divine power. Therefore the three principles of the opinion just mentioned, unknown to many, are enough, in my view, for a few to hold that the mind, placed in the body, works marvelous things outside itself by its own power.

What then? Let anyone ignorant of nature tell me whether bodily weight can be lightened by the operation of the mind. With two men bearing witness with me, I speak of a thing I experienced. When, as a young man, I was pursuing the study of letters, four of us were sleeping one night in a single bed. A companion of the same age rose from my side and, sleeping as he was accustomed to do, went about the house with his eyes closed, while the moon was shining in, on about the fifteenth day, as if awake. He climbed walls, and overcame the window by his agility. Still asleep, he crossed the bed a second and third time; he trod on us all with his feet, and we felt no greater weight than if a little mouse had touched us. Wherever his sleeping body moved, all the fastenings of the doors opened of their own accord. He entered the higher parts of the house very swiftly, and clung to the roofs like a sparrow. I speak of things I saw, not things heard by vague report.

These seem to be acts of the soul, not of the body; and the soul, so to speak, uses its own natural power almost freely when, the senses of the flesh being bound, it wanders outside the dwelling of the body. But since this material does not in every respect fit the question proposed, let us postpone the treatment of the causes of these marvels to another time. For we do not believe these things marvelous to the wise, who have understood very well the power and nobility of the human mind, since it is held back only by the interposition of the body, and in the rest is considered equal to the angels.

Finally, we pass over the various modes and kinds of fascinations, by which a greatly frenzied man produces effects outwardly very marvelous. A most strongly confident imagination can also do much to produce marvelous effects, whether it is borne toward a true object or toward one merely supposed. Hence, since there are so many kinds and modes of working marvels, it is not to be wondered at if Jews, Saracens, pagans, gentiles, and all the rest placed outside the faith of Christ, unbelievers who cannot work miracles through public righteousness, accomplish marvels either by the aid of demons or by artful industry. Nor does it escape me that by the same reasoning the miracles of the saints are attacked by the impious, as though they were not by the power of the Creator but rather by the involvement or substitution of the devil. Whoever truly believes that the Christian faith alone is true does not doubt that all the miracles of unbelievers are performed by the cooperation of demons. But if anyone rashly and stubbornly thinks the contrary, he shows himself to be an unbeliever, not a Christian.

On Sacred Scripture, the Fourth Question.

The fourth question of your most serene majesty was this: Why did almighty God make holy Scripture so new…

Qua ueteris testamenti mysteria fidei nostrae continentem, non dederit apertam, manifestam in omnibus uniformem et palā ad omnia sufficientem, sed inuoluta potius, et in multis locis aenyg matibus plenā. Multa enim ad perfectione fidei sunt necessaria, que in divinis scripturis non repereuntur sufficienter expressa. Ad hanc ma testatis tuae sacratissimae questione uidetur respondendum. Omnis scriptura divinitus inspirata perfectum divinitatis est opus ante tempus omne preordinatum, in tempore scriptum, nó se tus q̄ deus uoluit, qui ut scriberetur hominibus inspirauit Dei autem omnia perfecta sunt opera, ideoque cum scriptura de qua loqui mur dei sit opus, necessarium est eam in omnibus consiteri perfecta. Summus etenim arbiter deus cuius omnia perfecta sunt opera, sicvt uoluit et quem uoluit scripturis suis ordinem contulit, et excipientibus illas quemadmodu scriberent pro culdubio infudit. Sacra nanque scripturae tam omnipotens Deus auctoritatem et maiesta tem contulit, ut in eius comparatione omnia hu tus mundi uocabula deficiant, cum divina humanis propriè nequeant comprehendendi sermonibus 30 monibus. Divina igitur scriptura qua superficie verborum nescientibus appareat confusa, scientibus eam uidetur manifesta, quoniam nisi legatur illo spirito quo infusa hominibus creditur, ad eius intellectum minimè peruenitur. Aliter eam legit doctus qui carnis umbraculo de uanis desiderijs aestuat, & aliter intelligens quem exutum voluptatibus amor Dei ueraciter inflammat. Vnde mirum non est si homines carnaliter sapientes diuinas scripturas non intel=ligant, qui carnis voluptatib. obcoecati, dei spiri= tus dulcedinem nunquam perceperũt. Quemad modum si puerò prima literarũ elementa dif=centi uolumen exhibeas quodcunque scriptum, c̄ius character suo sit libello dissimilis cum lege=re nequiuerit scripturam ilico malam et non re=ele formatam exclamabit. Pari modo ad lectio=nem diuinarum scripturarum accedentes homi=nes carnaliter duntaxat sapientes, qui ea qua diuini spiritus sunt non capiunt, uicijs et temerite=se grauati cum suam ignorantiam et indignita=tem culpare debuissent scripturas quas no intel=ligũt sanctas reprehẽdũt. No enim passim oib=divinas licet interpretari scripturas, ne bestie contingens montem, lapidibus obruatur. Sursgunt nunc ordine praepostero plures qui omne uita suae tempus in litteris humanitatis consumpserunt, & seniores facti diuinas scripturas quas nunquam didicerunt perperam interpretantes non enucleant sed confundunt, & in proprio sensu discutiunt. Unde quicunque sacras scripturas non eo spiritu intelligunt quo scribentibus sunt infusae, uelamen ignorantiae et temeritatis super cordibus suis habent more iudaeorum expansum, & inde soepius uenenum perniciosi erroris hauriunt, unde in spiritu accedentes Dei humiles salutis poculum acceperunt. Non enim habetur doctrina coelestis in uerbis scripturarum sed in sensu, non in superficie sermonum, sed in intellectu, non in folis ornatae orationis, sed in occulto mysticae inspirationis. Hinc diuus papa Gregorius. Sacra inquit scriptura omnes huius mundi scientias, more locutionis suae longè transcendit, quoniam in uno eodemque sermone dum narrat textum, occultum prodit mysterium, & quemadmodum simplices superficie reuouet, ita sapientes mysterio exercet. Habet enim in publico unde paruulos nutriat.

Why Scripture, containing the mysteries of the Old Testament and of our faith, was not given open, manifest, everywhere uniform, and plainly sufficient for all things, but rather wrapped up and in many places full of enigmas. For many things necessary for the perfection of faith are not found sufficiently expressed in the divine Scriptures. To this most sacred question of your Majesty it seems one must reply.

All Scripture, inspired by God, is the perfect work of the Godhead, foreordained before all time, written in time, not otherwise than God willed, who inspired men that it should be written. But all God’s works are perfect; and therefore, since the Scripture of which we speak is God’s work, it is necessary to confess that it is perfect in all things. For God, the supreme judge, all whose works are perfect, gave to his Scriptures the order that he willed and as he willed, and without doubt infused into those who received them the manner in which they should write. For almighty God bestowed such authority and majesty upon the sacred Scriptures that, in comparison with them, all the words of this world fail, since divine things cannot properly be comprehended in human speech.

Therefore divine Scripture, although on the surface of its words it may appear confused to the ignorant, seems manifest to those who know it, since unless it is read in that Spirit by which it is believed to have been infused into men, one by no means arrives at an understanding of it. The learned man who burns with vain desires under the shelter of the flesh reads it in one way, and the understanding man whom the love of God truly inflames, stripped of pleasures, reads it in another. Hence it is no wonder if men who are wise according to the flesh do not understand the divine Scriptures, since, blinded by the pleasures of the flesh, they have never perceived the sweetness of God’s Spirit.

Just as, if you present to a boy learning the first elements of letters any written volume whose character is unlike that in his little book, when he cannot read the writing he will at once cry out that it is bad and not properly formed; in the same way, men who approach the reading of the divine Scriptures with only fleshly wisdom, who do not grasp the things that are of the divine Spirit, weighed down by vices and rashness, when they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, reproach the holy Scriptures which they do not understand. For it is not permissible for all indiscriminately to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest even a beast touching the mountain be overwhelmed with stones.

Now, in a perverse order, many arise who have spent the whole time of their life in humane letters and, having become old men, wrongly interpreting the divine Scriptures which they never learned, do not explain them but confuse them, and examine them according to their own sense. Hence whoever does not understand the sacred Scriptures by that Spirit by which they were infused into those who wrote them has a veil of ignorance and rashness spread over his heart in the manner of the Jews; and from the very place from which the humble, approaching in the Spirit of God, have received the cup of salvation, they very often drink the poison of pernicious error.

For heavenly doctrine is not contained in the words of the Scriptures but in the sense, not on the surface of the sayings but in the understanding, not in the leaves of ornate speech but in the hidden depth of mystical inspiration. Hence the holy Pope Gregory says: Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in the manner of its speech, because in one and the same discourse, while it narrates the text, it discloses the hidden mystery; and just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise with mystery. For it has openly that from which it may nourish little ones.

19
31 triat, & servat in occulto unde mentes sublimi- um in admirationem dulcedinis suspendat, quasi fluuius quidam mirabilis in quo et agnus sim- plex et paruulus ambulet, & elephas magnus natet. Et sanctus Augustinus super Genesim di- cit: Sic divina loquitur scriptura ut altitudine sua superbos irrideat, attêtos profunditate sua terreat, magnos uirtute pascat, et sua paruulos affabilitate nutriat. Maior enim est sacrae scri- pturae auctoritas, quam sit omnis ingenij huma- ni perspicacitas. Propterea quatenus ad carum uerum intellectum perueniatur, in primis pur- gandus est ab omni affectione carnali animus, implorandum sedulò cum humilitate diuina bo- nitatis auxilium, ut suo illuminet spiritu discen- tis intellectum. Auctoritati nang; diuinarũ scri- pturarum omnium colla subdenda sunt potesta- tum, & sicut inquit Diuus Hierony. nunquã sic adulandum est homini, ut sanctarum scriptura- rum ueritas negligatur, quaae tota in utroque testa- mento et in narratione gestorum est uera, in monitionibus recta, in promissionibus certa, & in comminationibus terribiliter metuenda. Quo circa non omribus datum est posse diuinarum scripturarum penetrare mysteria, sed illis dun taxat utcung; permittitur, quibus et amor continuat studium, & dei spiritus purgatis mentibus uerum confert intellectum. Quisquis autem caligine uiciorum est sordidus, quisquis mente tumida incedit superbus, quisquis de ueritate scripturarum Dei uel in parte uel in toto dubitat, nunquam ad earum intelligentiam se posse pertingere confidat. Dicit enim ipsius autoritas scripturae: quoniam nisi credideritis non intelligetis. Nostri est tarditas ingenij, nostri quoque impuritas desiderij, quotiens divinas scripturas non recte intelligimus, quando uidelicet uelamen perniciose occupationis super cordibus nostris manet expansum, quod non finit nos ad uerum peruenire intellectum. Hinc fit quod sensum quem spiritus sanctus divinis scripturis infudit non intelligimus, sed nuda scribentium uerba capientes in alium sensum retorquemus. Enimuero si mentes nostra a uicijs essent purgatae carnalibus, si per continuum sobrietatis studium ingenium exercitaretur in scripturis, si ea sanctis scripturis adhiberetur credulitas et reueretia qua dignitas requirit, luce clarius intelligeret omnis studi- sus, nihil sacris lectionibus inesse confusum, nihil dissonum, nihil inconueniens, nihil abs- urdum, aut sine iustissima ratione insertum. Omnia quidem divina loca scripturae sunt plena mysterijs, & quotiens aliquid in eis uide- tur obscurè positum, divina est prouidentia fa- etum, quatenus et studiosa mens necessarium habeat pietatis exercitium, & fides simplicium debitae reuerentia non amitteret locũ. Non igi tur à casu sed prouidentia sempiterna scriptu- ras sanctas in multis locis uoluit esse obscuras, quotenus tot abundaret mysterijs, quod sensibius inspirante dei spiritu catholicè à doctoribus explanatur. Nam ut sacer inquit Augustinus di uine scripturae obscuritas utilis est et multum proficia, propterea quod plures sentêtias ueri tatis parit et in lucẽ producit hominib. quia cũ alius hunc alius uero alium sensum catholice ea exponendo cruit, quam sit alta et profunda in- notescit. Vnde non existimet homo seculari lit- teratura tumidus quod sacram scripturam intel ligat, nisi prius uelamen superbie, & ois inordi nate concupiscentiae deponat. Secularis enim

…nourishes, and keeps hidden that by which it may hold the minds of the lofty suspended in wonder at its sweetness, like some marvelous river in which both the simple little lamb may walk and the great elephant may swim. And Saint Augustine says on Genesis: Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth terrifies the attentive, by its power feeds the great, and by its affability nourishes the little ones. For the authority of sacred Scripture is greater than all the keenness of human intellect.

Therefore, in order to arrive at its true understanding, the soul must first be cleansed of every carnal affection, and the help of divine goodness must be diligently implored with humility, so that by his Spirit he may enlighten the understanding of the learner. For the necks of all authorities must be bowed to the authority of the divine Scriptures; and, as Saint Jerome says, no one must ever be flattered in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected, which in both Testaments is wholly true in its narration of deeds, right in its admonitions, certain in its promises, and terribly to be feared in its threats. Therefore it is not given to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but only to those, in whatever measure it is permitted, in whom love sustains continual study, and to whose purified minds the Spirit of God grants true understanding.

But whoever is filthy with the darkness of vices, whoever walks proudly with a swollen mind, whoever doubts the truth of the Scriptures of God, whether in part or in whole, let him never trust that he can attain to their understanding. For the authority of Scripture itself says: Unless you believe, you will not understand. It is our slowness of intellect, and also our impurity of desire, whenever we do not understand the divine Scriptures rightly, namely when the veil of harmful occupation remains spread over our hearts, which does not allow us to come to true understanding. Hence it happens that we do not understand the meaning which the Holy Spirit has poured into the divine Scriptures, but, grasping the bare words of the writers, twist them to another meaning.

Indeed, if our minds were purified from carnal vices, if the intellect were exercised in the Scriptures through continual zeal for sobriety, if that belief and reverence were applied to the holy Scriptures which their dignity requires, every studious person would understand more clearly than light that there is nothing confused in the sacred readings, nothing discordant, nothing unsuitable, nothing absurd, or inserted without the most just reason. All passages of divine Scripture are indeed full of mysteries, and whenever anything in them seems to be set down obscurely, it has been done by divine providence, so that the studious mind may have the necessary exercise of piety, and the faith of the simple may not lose the place of due reverence.

Therefore it was not by chance, but by eternal providence, that he willed the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that they might abound in so many mysteries, which, by the inspiration of the Spirit of God, are expounded in a catholic sense by teachers. For, as holy Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is useful and very profitable, because it gives birth to many meanings of truth and brings them forth into the light for human beings; since, when one person draws out this meaning and another a different one by expounding it in catholic fashion, it becomes known how high and deep it is. Therefore let no one swollen with secular learning think that he understands sacred Scripture unless he first lays aside the veil of pride and of every disordered desire. For secular

20
litteratura maiusualet ad exercitandum ingenium, quam ad illuminandu ad ueram sapientiam intellectum. Est ergo sine dubio scriptura divina purgatis mentibus qui continuum exercitium divini timoris, et frequens studium lectio et manifesta et lucida, que sordidis et seculari sapientia inflatis confusa uidetur et obscura. Unde scripturas sanctas ille bene et recte intelligit, qui affectione purgata, in eorum studio frequens, sic eas exponit sicut ille qui scripsit. Nam si alio spiritu legantur, quam illo qui eas ut scriberentur inspirasse creditur, necesse est quod mens a vero intellectu penitus arceatur: Cum uero dissonantia in eis aliqua offendimus, non sensuum sed uerborum esse duntaxat intelligamus, qua non a cafu, sed prouidentia Dei ordinate nascitur, ut mens in scripturis (ne torpescat omnino) exercitata diutius roboretur. Dei nang; consilium falli non potest, sed divinae scripturae consilio voluntatis eius sunt scripturae, sequitur necessario, quod sint uera et nullatenus false. Homines fuerunt a qui bus divinae nobis scripturae traditae sunt, uerba certe humana consuetudine usitata. Scripserunt, 33 runt, quibus hoc significarent posteritati quod summa illa diuinitatis excellentia notum uoluit esse mortalibus. Vos igitur nunc qui seculari sapientiae dediti scripturas impugnatis diuinas dicite. Noui ac ueteris testamenti quam ut ueram auctenticam et sanctam christianorum su fcepit et ueneratur scripturam ecclesia, Vnde susceptam creditis? Ex deo, an ex hominibus? Si ex deo: quare uos ei non creditis? Omnis enim qui scripturam impugnat quam ex deo in spiratam credit, diuinae ordmationi manifestis simè resistit. Si autem ex hominibus est: quare vos promissam in ea salutem speratis aeternam, quam homo dare nō potest: Nisi forsitan per gatis dicere infani conficta omnia, & nihil re stare post fata quam cinerem, mentemque simul cum corpore subire interitū, qua professione non minus uos infanos demonstraret quã fatuos. Nā si in dominũ nostrum Iesum Christũ unigenitum filium dei ueraciter creditis, inspiratas à spiritu santo diuinas scripturas necessario dicetis. Quod si facti cum apostatis in reprobum sen sum confictas ab hominibus dixeritus, quam lon gè sitis à uera sapientia in tenebris errantes impiè demonstratis, Imperitos et temerarios judices vos esse palam ostenditis, qui scriptu- ram quam non intelligitis condemnatis. Verum quia familiarius est uobis sapientiam contem- nere quam discere, non est huius operis contra temeritatem imperitorum diutius mentem fati- gare. Hoc unum uos scire uolo, quoniam nemo intelligit nisi qui accipit, sed quia uos ne acci- piatis fordes affectionum interponitis, propte- rea intellectum uerae sapientiae non habetis. Omnipotens etenim deus illis per gratiam illu- minator adesse dignatur, qui carnalibus exuti desiderijs, interni amoris flagrant incendio, qui praeter deum nihil cupiunt in hoc mundo. Illis dei spiritus praesentia sua fert opem, quos in amore ueritatis radicatos inuenerit, & purga- tos ab omni aduentitio incognoscentiam omni- um introducit. Vere nang; diligentibus deum omnia sunt aperta, omnia nuda, omnia manife- sta, quoniam quisquis per amorem in fide Iesu Christi omnia creantem et gubernantem con- spicit, uniuersa quae sunt ei ad salutem necessa- ria cognoscit. At uero contra ab ignauis, im- probis epulon: b us, inu:dis, & iaris, incubonibus, fordidis

Secular learning has more power to exercise the intellect than to enlighten it for true wisdom. Therefore, without doubt, divine Scripture is clear and bright to purified minds through continual practice of the fear of God and frequent devotion to reading, though to filthy minds, swollen with worldly wisdom, it seems confused and obscure. Hence he understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly who, with purified affection and constant in their study, explains them in the same sense as the one who wrote them. For if they are read in any spirit other than that by which he is believed to have inspired them to be written, the mind must be wholly shut out from true understanding.

But when we meet with any discordance in them, let us understand that it belongs only to the words, not to the meanings; and this arises in ordered fashion not by chance but by the providence of God, so that the mind, exercised longer in the Scriptures, may be strengthened and not grow altogether sluggish. For God’s counsel cannot be deceived; but the divine Scriptures are Scriptures by the counsel of his will. It follows necessarily that they are true and in no way false. They were men by whom the divine Scriptures were handed down to us, and certainly words customary in human usage. They wrote with words by which they might signify to posterity what that supreme excellence of divinity wished to be known to mortals.

Therefore you now, who are devoted to worldly wisdom and attack the divine Scriptures, say: the Scripture of the New and Old Testament, which the Church has received and venerates as the true, authentic, and holy Scripture of Christians, from where do you believe it was received? From God, or from men? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks Scripture which he believes to be inspired by God most plainly resists the divine ordinance. But if it is from men, why do you hope in it for the eternal salvation promised there, which man cannot give? Unless perhaps, madmen, you go on to say that all things are fabricated, and that nothing remains after death except ashes, and that the mind perishes together with the body; by such a profession you would show yourselves no less insane than foolish.

For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit. But if, made one with apostates in a reprobate mind, you say they were fabricated by men, you impiously show how far you are from true wisdom, wandering in darkness. You openly reveal yourselves to be ignorant and rash judges, since you condemn a Scripture which you do not understand.

But because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it is not the purpose of this work to weary the mind any longer against the rashness of the ignorant. This one thing I wish you to know: no one understands unless he receives; but because you place the filth of your affections in the way, so that you may not receive, therefore you do not have the understanding of true wisdom.

For almighty God deigns to be present as illuminator through grace to those who, stripped of carnal desires, burn with the fire of inward love, who desire nothing in this world except God. To them the Spirit of God brings help by his presence; those whom he finds rooted in the love of truth and purified from every foreign thing, he brings into the knowledge of all things. For to those who truly love God all things are open, all things naked, all things manifest, since whoever through love beholds in faith Jesus Christ, creating and governing all things, knows all things that are necessary for his salvation. But, on the contrary, from the slothful, wicked feasters, the envious and greedy, [unclear], the filthy...
