Constat igitur manifestè q tota potestas male- ficarum in qua tam miranda faciunt daemonibus à domino deo limitata cceditur, & quando ille non permittit, nihil operantur. DE PERMISSIONE DI- uina. Quaestio septima. S Eptima Quaestio serenissima maiestatis tue, ista fuit. Quare deus cum sit iu- stus et uindex malorum, tanta maleficia in perniciem humani generis fieri permittit, quibus non solum peccatores, sed etiam inmo- centes multi pereunt grauiter cruciati. Ad hanc quaestionem taliter me dudum coram maiestate tua constitutum memini respondisse. Optimus deus iustus et rectus, pius et miseri- cors, quicquid permittit, iuste permittit, quaeni am iustus est, & non est apud illum iniquitas, sed omnia in uero iudicio quae fiunt aut facit, aut permittit. Cum ergo quaeritur quare deus mala fieri permittat, respondemus. Ideo permittet, quia iustus est. Nū uideatur maiestati tuae et Caesar quam dedimus absurda responso, quoniam divina bonitati non praejudicat ulla tenus, quod mala fieri iustissima ratione permittit, potius autem praejudicaret si mala in praesenti modo fieri non permetteret. Enimvero si nō permetteret fieri mala, iam homo peccare non posset, esset certe inpeccabilis quod eius natura non conuenit, cui ab initio liberũ arbitrium conditor omnium dedit. Homo etenim creatura cui sit et non creator, est necessario tam ad bonum convertibilis quam ad malum, cuius esse dependet à summo creaturarum opifice omnium, quemadmodum à causa sui esse omne causatum. Creare vero solideo relictũ est qui est incorruptibilis et sempiternus, corruptibile aut omne necessario deficit, conse uatur autem bonitate creatoris quae diu cause influentiā non amittit. Vnde fieri nee potuit, nec decuit quod homo ex conditione sua naturae crearetur inpeccabilis, quo solus gau det naturaliter opifex omnium deus, qui est incommutabilis et sempiternus. Quoties uero confertur homini ut peccare non posse uideatur. tur, nec libertas arbitrii tollitur, nec possibilis simpliciter auffertur, sed voluntas in bono confirmatur. Et quotienscumque hunc donum confertur creaturae, munus est gratiae non naturae. Dicit enim scriptura. Deus ab initio creavit hominem et reliquit eum in manu consilij sui. Nam proprie loquendo esse non potest, ut homo moralis in originali disiplcentia conceptus et librum habeat arbitrium, et non possit committere peccatum. Dicit enim sanctissimus praeful Augustinus. Prima libertas voluntatis erat posse peccare, nouissima erit in gloria multo magis, non posse peccare. Itaque si homo peccare non posset, proprie voluntatis sua dominum non haberet. Unde quamuis omnipotens Deus peccatum non uelit, peccare tamen homines et malum facere iustè permittit, quatenus libertate arbitrii permanente et virtus boni operis meritum, et pravitas voluntaria recipiat, quod fecerit malum. Nemo enim aut bene facit aut peccat inuitus. Iustè igitur omnipotens Deus peccare et malum facere homines permittebit, quibus a principio libertatem arbitrii concessit. Sunt autem multae rationes a sanctis doctis Aoribus dudum assignate, quare omnipotens maleficia tanta fieri per daemonum cooperatorem permittat, quarum ordine necessario breuiter faciemus mentionem. Prima est ut divinae manifestetur excellentia potestatis qui solus est incommutabilis, & supra omne longe positionem. Omnis autem creatura mutabilis, ad incommutabilem creatorē nullā habet comparationem. Vnde in numeris legitur: Non est deus quasi homo ut mentiatur, nec ut filius hominis ut mutetur. In Esaia quoque diicitur: Deus fidelis absque iniquitate iustus et reetus. In libro etiam Thobiae scribitur: Iustus es domine, & omnia iudicia tua uera sunt, et omnes uiae tuae misericordia veritas et iuditium. Et in libro sancti Iob legimus: Absit a deo impietas, & ab omnipotente iniquitas. Opus enim hominis reddet ei, et iuxta uias singularum restituet eiis. Omnis igitur homo qui suam ignorationem et infirmitatem recte intelligit, quam sit nihil comparatus ad creatorem suum patēter agnoscit. Iuste namque deus permittit peccare hominē, quo et libertas continuetur arbitrii, & excellētia hominibus innotescat magni dei.

Some of the terrestrial spirits also, as has been said, serve sorceresses; yet, being ranked in a lower degree, they can by no means bring about those greater acts of sorcery. It is therefore manifestly clear that the whole power of sorceresses, by which they do such astonishing things, is granted to demons in limited measure by the Lord God, and when he does not permit it, they accomplish nothing.

On divine permission. The seventh question.

This was the seventh question of your most serene majesty: Why does God, since he is just and the avenger of evils, permit such great acts of sorcery to be done for the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners but also many innocent people perish, grievously tormented?

I remember that, when I stood before your majesty, I answered this question in this way. The best God, just and upright, kind and merciful, whatever he permits, permits justly, because he is just, and there is no iniquity with him; rather, all things that happen he either does or permits in true judgment. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evils to be done, we answer: he permits them because he is just. Nor, Caesar, should the answer we have given seem absurd to your majesty, since it in no way prejudices the divine goodness that he permits evils to be done for a most just reason; rather, it would prejudice it if he did not permit evils to be done in the present state.

For truly, if he did not permit evils to be done, man could no longer sin; he would certainly be impeccable, which does not befit his nature, since from the beginning the Creator of all things gave him free choice. For man, since he is a creature and not the Creator, is necessarily able to be turned both to good and to evil, since his being depends on the supreme maker of all creatures, just as every caused thing depends on the cause of its being. But to create has been left to God alone, who is incorruptible and everlasting; every corruptible thing necessarily fails, yet it is preserved by the goodness of the Creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. Hence it neither could nor ought to have happened that man, by the condition of his nature, should be created impeccable, since God alone, the maker of all things, who is unchangeable and everlasting, naturally possesses this. But whenever it is granted to man that he seems unable to sin, the freedom of choice is not removed, nor is possibility simply taken away, but the will is confirmed in good. And whenever this gift is conferred on a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature.

For Scripture says: “God created man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel.” For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, should both have free choice and be unable to commit sin. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: “The first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the last, in glory, will be much greater: to be unable to sin.” And so, if man could not sin, he would not have mastery over his own will. Therefore, although almighty God does not will sin, he nevertheless justly permits human beings to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of choice remains, both the virtue of a good work may receive its reward and voluntary wickedness may receive what evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly. Therefore almighty God justly permits human beings to sin and to do evil, since from the beginning he granted them freedom of choice.

Many reasons have long since been assigned by the holy doctors why the Almighty permits such great acts of sorcery to be done through the cooperation of demons; we shall necessarily mention them briefly in order.

The first is so that the excellence of divine power may be made manifest, for he alone is unchangeable and far above every position [unclear]. Every creature, however, is changeable and has no comparison with the unchangeable Creator. Hence it is read in Numbers: God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. In Isaiah also it is said: God is faithful, without iniquity, just and upright. In the book of Tobit too it is written: You are just, Lord, and all your judgments are true, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And in the book of holy Job we read: Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will repay a man’s work to him, and according to the ways of each he will restore to them. Therefore every man who rightly understands his own ignorance and weakness plainly recognizes what a nothing he is compared with his Creator. For God justly permits man to sin, both so that freedom of choice may continue and so that the excellence of the great God may become known to human beings.

30
Secunda ratio est, ut imperscrutabilis dei sapientia innotescat mortalibus, quae novit ex nostris malis elicere bonum, cum unius peccatum alterius facit esse meritum ad virtutis incrementum. Nam si malu fieri nō permitteret, quis no strū intelligeret bonum? Facit enim deus bonum ordinat, mala vero non facit, sed ab impiis facta ne inordinate ueniant ipfe disponit. Neque malicia hominum Dei uoluntatem impedit, neque potest homo quicquam quod Deus non permittit. Tertia uero causa est quod omnipotens fiesri maleficia permittit ut manifestet suam clemẽ tissimā bonitatem in eos qui peccaue:ũt et ege runtpoenitêtiam, quam nullatenus posset osten dere, si creaturam non permitteret peccare. Nam si nullus esset peccator, nec deus posset ef se miserator. Sed quoniam in multis offendimus omnes, ubique deus inuenit quod remittat, ubique reus occurrit, in quo suam misericordiam pius cōditor ostendat. Vnde saectus praeful Augusti. Si leuis morbus esset cōtemneretur medicus, non quaereretur, si medicus non quaereretur, morbus non finiretur, ideo ubi abundauit pec= catum abudauit et gratia, que sola discernitre demptos et perditis, quos in unum coaceruat massa perditionis, ab origine ducta creationis. Est ergo misericordia domini super omnia opera eijs. Quarta vero ratio divinae permissionis est, ut iusticia creatoris in eos declaretur, qui peccaverunt, & non egerunt paenitentiam, quoniam se omnes benefacere et nemo peccaret, nihil habet dei iustitia quod puniret. Ut ergo iusticia locum habeat, divina permissione creatura peccat. Iustus enim est dominus, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera voluntatis sue. Quinta ratio est dignitas conditionis humanae, quia si deus non permetteret peccare hominem, brutis uideretur deterior, quae nulla impellente violentia naturae motibus libere utitur. Nam si ratione bruta careant, liberum tamen naturae motum habent, quem sequuntur, in quorum comparatione homo uideretur inferioris conditionis, si liberi non haberet arbitrii voluntatis. Permisit autem homini deus voluntatem liberam, qui nec reges imperant, nec principes. Sexta ratio est laus meriti constatiae humanae 52 virtutis, quādo iustū virū propterea laudamus, quia cu potuisset transgressi nō est trāsgressus, sed gratia dei adiuuante in bonē voluntatis con stantia permansit. Septima ratio quare omnipotens deus permit tat dēmones tanta maleficia intercursu malefī carum facere, est ut illi qui contempta ueritate delectantur mendacio, per muentcrem menda cij diabolū seducti penitus decipiātur. Dignū es enim ut incātatores atque maleficā qui salutaria Christi documenta sequi despiciunt, à dēmoni bus decepti omnes ad inferos demergātur in āter nū puniēdi. Suffragiū à dēmonibus totius huma ni generis hostibus expetūt, & saluatorē mundi quē solū adorare debuerāt contēnunt. Iustū est enim ut is qui ueritate spontanea voluntate dese rens adhaeret mendacio, in interitum à diabolo praecipitetur. Octaua causa est manifestatio di uīnae potestatis cuius potentia et uirtus est super omnem creaturā. Enimuero cu deus omnipotens aliuando magna permittit diabolo, & parua quaeda denegat, quā sit infirmus humani generis hostis, & diuina maiestati subiectus in omnibus manifestat. Nihil enim à se ipso potest dia G 4. bolus, sed omnia que facit, deo permittente facit. Causa igitur omnium prima, propter quod omnipotens deus fieri maleficia permittit injusticia est, qua libertatem quam creatura semel a principio contulit, ordine inviolabili custodit. Verum quia potestas creaturae omnis a suo creatoris dependentis restricta est et limitata, nec diabolum omne quod uult posse manifestum est, nec hominem uoluntate quantumlibet depraudent. Voluntas quidem est libera, sed potestas certis et necessarijs gradibus limitata. Quoniam quidem si daemones possent omne quod uolunt, nihil tutum in humanis permaneret, sed la befactarent omnia. Ligatam uero potestatem daemonum hystoria sancti lob manifesto demoni strat exemplo, quem non amplius tentare Satan audebat, quam ei fuerat dispensatione divina permissum. Nemo enim in praesenti mundo quantumlibet iustus aut fortis daemonum furori posset resistere, si pro eorum arbitrio libera semper nocendi possent uti potestate. Ante uero dominicam passionem maiore quam postea libertate utebantur potestatis, sed Christo mortem pro nobis in ara crucis gustante, ualde iam deire=

The second reason is that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, which knows how to draw good from our evils, when it makes the sin of one person become the merit of another for the increase of virtue. For if he did not permit evil to be done, which of us would understand the good? For God makes and orders good things; he does not make evils, but when they have been done by the impious, he himself disposes them so that they may not come about in a disorderly way. Nor does the malice of men hinder the will of God, nor can man do anything that God does not permit.

The third cause is that the Almighty permits evil deeds to be done so that he may manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and have done penance, which he could in no way show if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, God could not be one who shows mercy. But since we all offend in many things, everywhere God finds something to forgive; everywhere a guilty person presents himself, in whom the kind Creator may show his mercy. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: If the disease were slight, the physician would be despised; he would not be sought; if the physician were not sought, the disease would not be ended. Therefore, where sin abounded, grace also abounded, which alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, heaps together into one. Therefore the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason for divine permission is that the justice of the Creator may be declared against those who have sinned and have not done penance, because if all did good and no one sinned, the justice of God would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have a place, the creature sins by divine permission. For the Lord is just, and he will render to each according to the works of his will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition, because if God did not permit man to sin, man would seem worse than the beasts, which, with no violence driving them, freely use the motions of nature. For although brute beasts lack reason, nevertheless they have a free motion of nature which they follow; in comparison with them man would seem to be of a lower condition if he did not have the will of free choice. But God permitted man a free will, over which neither kings nor princes command.

The sixth reason is the praise of the merit of constancy in human virtue, when we praise a just man because, although he could have transgressed, he did not transgress, but, with the grace of God helping him, remained steadfast in a good will.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits demons to do such great evil deeds through the agency of witches is that those who, having despised the truth, delight in falsehood may, seduced by the devil, the inventor of falsehood, be utterly deceived. For it is fitting that enchanters and evildoers who scorn to follow the saving teachings of Christ should all, deceived by demons, be plunged down to hell to be punished forever. They seek help from demons, the enemies of the whole human race, and they despise the Savior of the world, whom alone they ought to have adored. For it is just that one who, deserting the truth by his own voluntary will, clings to falsehood should be hurled by the devil into destruction.

The eighth cause is the manifestation of divine power, whose might and strength are over every creature. Indeed, when almighty God sometimes permits great things to the devil and denies him certain small things, he shows how weak the enemy of the human race is, and how subject in all things to the divine majesty. For the devil can do nothing of himself, but all that he does, he does with God permitting it. Therefore the first cause of all, on account of which almighty God permits evil deeds to be done, is justice, by which he preserves in an inviolable order the freedom which he once bestowed on the creature from the beginning. But because every power of the creature, dependent on its Creator, is restricted and limited, it is clear that the devil cannot do everything he wishes, nor can man, however depraved in will. The will is indeed free, but power is limited by fixed and necessary degrees. For if demons could do everything they wish, nothing among human affairs would remain safe, but they would shake all things to ruin. The history of holy Job shows by a clear example the bound power of demons, for Satan did not dare to tempt him beyond what had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. For no one in the present world, however just or strong, could resist the fury of demons if, at their own discretion, they could always use a free power of harming. Before the Lord’s Passion, however, they enjoyed greater freedom of power than afterward; but when Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, it was already greatly [unclear].

53 deinceps eorum est imminuta potestas. Salvatore in evangelio dicente. Nunc princeps mundi eijcietur foras. Etenim Christi humilitas et perseverantia sanctorum audaciam daemonum ualde restringerunt, ita quod incitores malorum recte nuncupari possunt, impulsores vero minimè. Nec imualesceret contra nos diabolus, nisi uires ex nostris peccatis acciperet. Hinc nos scriptura admonet, dicens. Resistite diabo lo et fugiet a uobis. Et iterum: Nolite locu dare diabolo. Concludendo igitur sermonem ad intelligentiam propositae questionis, quare deus fieri tot maleficia permittat, rationes credo sufficienter manifestas. Nam si uoluntas daemonum semper sit iniqua, potestas tamen nun= quam potest esse inuista, quoniam quod male uult ex proprio habet arbitrio, quod autem male facere potest solum habet a deo. Et haec quantum ad eos pertinet qui mala faciunt dicit a sunt. Sed quare omnipotens deus permittit daemones laedere homines medio maleficiarum qui in nomine sanctae trinitatis baptisati sunt, et fideliter cre dunt in unigenitum filium eius dominum nostrum Iesum Christum? Nam si malos peruerfus, et infideles in corpore et in rebus tantum ledere possent, coercerentur vero ab accessu et lesione bonorum atque fidelium, permissionis iustum recte uideretur esse iudicium. Nunc autem frequentius boni et innocentes daemonii maleficijs infirmatur, & quandoque etiam uita priuantur, ut silentio iactura rerum temporalium quam sē pe maleficiati patiuntur transeamus, multis uenit in scrupulum cur ista permittat omnipotens qui nihil permittit inuuste. Huius propositae questionis non alias quam à priscis atque catholicis accepi doctoribus quanto potero breuiter necessarias per ordinem assignabo rationes. Et prima quidem ratio est probatio fidei Christianorum et experientia integritatis, ut maleficijs daemonum flagellati discant in passionibus carnis, quam fidē et dilectionem ad deum habeant in abscondito mentis. In prosperis esse longanimem non est difficile, sed in adversis cum humili patientia à saluatore fidelium praestolari auxilium, non mollium est sed fortiũ et uere fidelũ Christianorũ. Didi cit in sua tribulatione sanctissimus Iob, quātam in deũ fidei haberet constantiā, qui antea in trāe quili= 54 quillitate custodierat sine tentationis iaculo pietatem. Hinc simul notandu q. illi quos doemonum uel hominum maleficia quom docunque fecerunt infirmos, qui pro sanitate recuperanda ma lesicos et incantatores quoscunque uel accedũt, uel consulunt, sive per se, sive per alios, contra dei et ecclesiae praecepta faciunt, & neque fidem in deum habent ueram, neque dilectionem. Sanita tem quippe moriturae carnis deo praeferunt, & salutem nō à Christo sed à diabolo et eius mini- stro quaerunt. Malunt enim in nomine diaboli fa ni sed infoeliciter uiuere, qua hic p Christi amo re modicũ pati, & postea cum eo in perpetuum gaudere. Qui uero maleficos nō accedit, ppte- rea quoniam deus prohibuit, malens uiuere cum obseruatiae mandatorũ dei in egestate et aegritu dine qua contra deũ in divitijs et corporis sane tate, ille deũ ueraciter diligit, & integritatem Christianae fidei recte custodit. Non sunt inter Christianos tollerandi ô sacratissime Caesar ho- mines mente corrupti et reprobì circa fidem, qui per maleficia curant maleficiatos, qui furta ministerio doemonum revelant et adulter- ria, qui lapidum aut speculorum inspectione proae

Thereafter their power was diminished, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” For the humility of Christ and the perseverance of the saints have greatly restrained the boldness of demons, so that they can now rightly be called inciters of evils, but by no means compellers. Nor would the devil grow strong against us unless he received strength from our sins. Hence Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” And again: “Do not give place to the devil.”

Therefore, in concluding the discussion for understanding the proposed question, why God permits so many acts of witchcraft to be done, I believe the reasons have been made sufficiently clear. For although the will of demons is always wicked, their power can never be unlimited, because what a demon wills wickedly he has from his own free choice, but what he is able to do wickedly he has only from God. And these things have been said as far as concerns those who do evil.

But why does almighty God permit demons, through the agency of works of witchcraft, to harm people who have been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity and who faithfully believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? For if they could harm only the wicked, the perverse, and unbelievers in body and possessions, but were restrained from access to and injury of the good and faithful, the judgment of the permission would rightly seem just. But now, since more often the good and innocent are weakened by demonic works of witchcraft, and sometimes are even deprived of life, to pass over in silence the loss of temporal goods which those bewitched often suffer, it comes as a scruple to many why the Almighty permits these things, he who permits nothing unjustly.

I shall set out in order, as briefly as I can, the necessary reasons for this proposed question, which I have received from none other than the ancient and Catholic doctors. The first reason is the testing of Christians’ faith and the proving of their integrity, so that, when scourged by the works of demons, they may learn in the sufferings of the flesh what faith and love toward God they possess in the hidden place of the mind. To be patient in prosperity is not difficult; but in adversity to await with humble patience help from the Savior of the faithful is not the mark of the soft, but of the strong and truly faithful Christians. In his tribulation most holy Job learned how great a constancy of faith toward God he had, he who previously in tranquillity had preserved piety without the dart of temptation.

Hence it must also be noted that those whom works of witchcraft by demons or by men have in any way made ill, and who, in order to recover health, either approach or consult witches and any enchanters, whether by themselves or through others, act against the commandments of God and of the Church, and have neither true faith in God nor love. For they prefer the health of their mortal flesh to God, and seek salvation not from Christ but from the devil and his minister. For they prefer to be healthy in the name of the devil and live unhappily, rather than to suffer a little here for the love of Christ and afterward rejoice with him forever. But whoever does not approach witches because God has forbidden it, preferring to live in poverty and sickness while observing the commandments of God rather than against God in riches and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly preserves the integrity of the Christian faith.

Among Christians, most sacred Caesar, men corrupted in mind and reprobate concerning the faith must not be tolerated: those who cure the bewitched by works of witchcraft, who reveal thefts and adulteries by the ministry of demons, who by inspection of stones or mirrors [unclear].

32
pranunciant futura. Non exaudi viiillos precor qui diuinarum legum ignari, huiusmodi minif- tros daemonum imperio tuo existimant utiles, propterea quod maleficio nouerunt maleficia dissoluere, quoniam ista pernicios a curatio cor porum, mortem inducit animarum, & facit ho- mines à deo creature omnium recedere, & im- pijs a apostatis daemonibus adhaerere, cum qui- bus post mortem damnabuntur in aeternum. Secunda ratio quare omnipotens deus male ficio laedi permittat innocentes, est augmentum meritorum, ut uidelicet probata eorum in tribu latione patientia, coronam gloriae in coelo dig- niorem mereat. Nam ut sacer inquit Augus. Homo sibi ignotus est quid ferre poscit quid non poscit, aliquando metuit se non posse quod tamē potest, cum accedit tentatio quasi interroga- ter quidam, homo inuenitur à se ipso, qui pri- us latens nesciebat seipsum. Diuus Archiapos- tolus Petrus, antequam superuenisset ei ten- tatio, & latebat et alics quam esset inconsi- deratus et infirmus, accessit illa et apparuit, infirmitas qua latebat. Maxima igitur hominis probatio tentatio est, sacra testante scriptu- ra 55 ra. Vasa figuli probat fornax, & homines iustos tentatio tribulationis. Facilis est in prosperitate patientia, quoniam mentem nulla pulsat adversa. Multae autem tribulationes iustorum, sed de omnibus liberabit eos Dominus nostror Iesus Christus. Tertia diuina permissionis ratio est humilitatis custodia, quatenus homo fidelis et iustus deum semper timeat, & nunquam de sua fortitudine vel iustitia praesumat. Hinc de reprobis dicit scriptura. In labore hominum non sunt, & cum hominibus non flagellabuntur. Ideonuit eos superbia, operti sunt iniquitate et impietate sua, prodyt quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum. Miserentis dei est quod homines bonos et iustos interdum permittit aduerstatibus concuti, quos nouit in prosperis non posse humiliari. Multos enim tribulatio fecit humiles, quos secunda reddidissent elatos. Deniq maleficiarum timidia imaginatio facit bonum hominem timere deum suum, & eius sedulo inuocare auxilium, quo munitus contra daemonum incursus, se pos sit confidere tutum. Nemo autem superbus et presumens de viribus suis a maleficijs daemoni se Se tutum existimet, quoniam quem inflatum suis perbia dei protectio deservit, doemonum malefici cys procul dubio patescit. Quarta ratio est, ut honorũ malorumque discre tio habeatur. Dicit enim de bonis ac deo dilectis hominibus scriptura in actibus apostolorum, quoniam per multas tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum dei. Et sanctus Christi ama tor Paulus in quadam epistola dicit. Omnes qui uolunt in Christo pie uivere, persecutionem patientur. Sapientissimus quoque rex Salomon in prouerbijs dicit. Quem diligit dominus cor ripit, & quasi pater in filio complacet sibi. Res Christiano nimis gloriosa, pro dei amore pa tienter tolerare aduersa, siue à malis hominibus inferantur siue à doemonibus. Datur enim po testas diabolo eiusque ministris ledendi homines bonos et iustos, non in eorum confusionem sicut petrones existimant, sed in maximam po tius et certam animae consolationem. Enimue ro cum bene uivit homo iustus neminem laedit, neminem offendit, nulli facit iniuriam, deum suum toto corde diligit, timet et veneratur, omni sollicitudine mandata eius custodiens, & 56 nihilominus tribulatur a malefiscis, siue in cora pore, siue in rebus, siue in utroq, uere beatus est homo ille, quoniam cum probatus fuerit ac cipiet coronam uita, quam promisit deus his qui diligunt eum. Omnis qui recte utuit in unitate fidei catholicae ecclesie Christianorum, & ma la in hoc mundo recipiens pro dei amore pa tienter tolerat, certum est signum quod in dei gratia saluandus perseverat. Quo circa de malis et reprobis ita scriptum legimus. Quare impii uiuunt, subleuati sunt, confortatiq duitijs Domus eorum securae sunt et pacate, et non est virga dei super illos, ducunt in bonis dies suos, & in puncto ad inferna descendunt. Manife stum enim damnationis est signum si hic male uinas in peccatis et uicijs deo contrarius et in bonis fortune corporis et sanitate prosperatus. Quinta ratio quod omnipotens permittit ho mines bonos et iustos tribulari a malis et re probis, est propter mentis omnimodam pur gationem. Nam sicut scriptura dicit: non est homo iustus in terra qui faciat bonum et non peccet. Sed cum deus nullum peccatum transeat impunitum, ordinat iustis hominibus per misericora

who foretell future things. Do not listen, I beg you, to those men who, ignorant of the divine laws, think ministers of demons of this kind useful to your rule because they know how to undo sorceries by sorcery; for that pernicious healing of bodies brings death upon souls, and makes men withdraw from God, the creator of all, and cling to impious apostate demons, with whom after death they will be damned forever.

The second reason why Almighty God permits the innocent to be harmed by sorcery is the increase of merits, so that their patience, proved in tribulation, may deserve a worthier crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says, a man is unknown to himself, what he can bear and what he cannot bear; sometimes he fears that he cannot do what nevertheless he can. When temptation comes, as a kind of questioner, a man is discovered by himself, who before, being hidden, did not know himself. The blessed arch-apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others as to how rash and weak he was; when it came, the weakness that had lain hidden appeared. Therefore temptation is the greatest testing of a man, as sacred Scripture bears witness: the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men. Patience is easy in prosperity, because no adversity strikes the mind. But many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from them all our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.

The third reason for divine permission is the preservation of humility, so that the faithful and righteous man may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or righteousness. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: They are not in the toil of men, and they will not be scourged with men. Therefore pride has held them; they are covered with their own iniquity and impiety; their iniquity has come forth as if from fatness. It belongs to the mercy of God that he sometimes permits good and righteous men to be shaken by adversities, whom he knows cannot be humbled in prosperity. For tribulation has made many humble whom favorable circumstances would have rendered proud. Finally, the fearful thought of sorceries makes a good man fear his God and diligently invoke his help, fortified by which he can trust that he is safe against the assaults of demons. But let no proud man, presuming upon his own strength, think himself safe from the sorceries of the demon, because he whom, puffed up by pride, the protection of God abandons, without doubt lies open to the sorceries of demons.

The fourth reason is so that there may be a distinction between good and bad people. For Scripture says of good men beloved by God, in the Acts of the Apostles, that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. And Saint Paul, lover of Christ, says in a certain epistle: All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. The most wise King Solomon also says in Proverbs: The Lord corrects whom he loves, and, like a father, he takes pleasure in his son. It is a very glorious thing for a Christian to endure adversities patiently for the love of God, whether they are inflicted by evil men or by demons. For power is given to the devil and his ministers to harm good and righteous men, not for their destruction, as [unclear] think, but rather for the greatest and sure consolation of the soul. For indeed, when a righteous man lives well, harms no one, offends no one, does injury to no one, loves, fears, and venerates his God with his whole heart, keeping his commandments with all solicitude, and nevertheless is troubled by sorcerers, whether in body, or in possessions, or in both, that man is truly blessed, because when he has been proved he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him. Everyone who lives rightly in the unity of the faith of the Catholic Church of Christians, and patiently endures the evils he receives in this world for the love of God, has a certain sign that he perseveres in the grace of God and will be saved. Therefore we read that it is written thus of the evil and reprobate: Why do the impious live, have they been raised up and strengthened with riches? Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them; they spend their days in good things, and in a moment they go down to hell. For it is a manifest sign of damnation if here you live wickedly in sins and vices, opposed to God, and prosper in the goods of fortune and in bodily health.

The fifth reason why the Almighty permits good and righteous men to be troubled by the evil and reprobate is because of the complete purification of the mind. For, as Scripture says, there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin. But since God lets no sin pass unpunished, he ordains for righteous men, through mercy

ricordiam pro eorum delictis poenas temporales, impijs uerò et reprobis per iustitiam aeternas. Commutat ergò ex misericordia poenitentibus poenam aeternam in temporalem, quam uel in hoc mundo patiantur necessarium est, uel post morte in purgatorio. Verũ quia purgatory tormenta sunt horrenda atque grauissima misericors deus poenitentes quos diligit in hac uita purgare uarijs modis consueuit, per incomo da diversarum in corpore et in rebus tribulationum. Profunt enim maleficia impiorum bonis et iustis hominibus ad medelam, ipsis autem inferentibus ad damnationem. Sexta ratio est ut homo per incursus doemonum maleficatus revocetur ad poenitentiam, et proponat in corde suo necessaria uite emendationem. Omnipotens etenim deus non subito, cu peccamus immittit uindicatam, sed usque ad praefinitum tempus nostram expectat emedationem. Si uero poenitentiam agere neglexerimus uenit ad nos uindex malorum, quando non putamus, qui nos peccatores in tranquilitate poenitendo recognoscere contempsimus, in tribulatione serò tandem recognoscemus. Denique permittit maleficio quosdam ad mortem impelli ut ampu- tetur eis peccandi licentia, qua fuerant abusu- ri diutius in uita permissti. Hinc de uiro iusto di cit scriptura. Raptus est ne malicia mutaret in- tellectum eius, & ne filio deciperet animam eius. Octuaratio divinae permissionis est, ut homines sacramenta venerentur ecclesiae, qua magnam habent uirtutem contra omnia male- ficia malignorum spirituum. Raro enim male- ficijs daemonum leditur, qui sacramenta et ri- tus ecclesiae cathelicae debito cum honore uene- ratur. Et propria maleficularum confessione sa- pius audiuimus, quod missarum auditio et usus rerum benedictarum ab ecclesia multum insir- ment daemonum potestates. Neque enim frustra benedicuntur in ecclesia dei, sed ut sint qua diui divina protectionis munimen daemonibus osten dant metuenda signacula. De pueris uero et infantibus, qui in Christo renati maleficijs da- monum uel hominum quandoque necantur, non dubitamus quin divina providentia hoc fieri permittat eis in salutem, qua omnia nouit in melius ordinare mortalibus. Saepe tamen con- tingit infantes maleficijs perire propter deli- ga parentum. De Providentia Dei, Quae- stio Octaua. O Ctua serenitatis tuae questio ista fuit: An ratione probari queat naturali, quemadmodum et sanctis scripturis, deum habere curam humanarum rerum et actionum, eorumque omnium et singulorum qua geruntur in mundo certam et infallibilem providentiam. Ad hanc questionem ita me memini re- pondisse: Mundus totus, coelum et terra et om nia que in eis sunt, divina sunt providentia subiecta, cuius uoluntate et imperio ab initio in esse producta fuerunt. Nihil est enim in to=

...mercy, temporal punishments for their offenses, but to the impious and reprobate, by justice, eternal punishments. Therefore, out of mercy, he changes eternal punishment for the penitent into temporal punishment, which they must necessarily suffer either in this world or after death in purgatory. But because the torments of purgatory are dreadful and very grievous, merciful God is accustomed to purge in this life, in various ways, the penitents whom he loves, through the discomfort of diverse tribulations in body and in possessions. For the harmful works of the impious profit good and righteous people as a remedy, but for those who inflict them they lead to damnation.

The sixth reason is so that a person harmed by the assaults of demons may be called back to repentance and may resolve in his heart upon the necessary amendment of life. For almighty God does not immediately send vengeance when we sin, but waits for our amendment until the appointed time. But if we have neglected to do penance, the avenger of evils comes to us when we do not expect it; we sinners, who in tranquility scorned to recognize ourselves by repenting, will at last, though late, recognize ourselves in tribulation. Hence the holy prophet speaks in the person of God, saying: “If his children forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with stripes; but my mercy I will not scatter from them, nor will I harm them in my truth.”

The seventh reason why almighty God permits the harmful works of demons to prevail against the good and innocent is so that an excessively unchecked opportunity for sinning may be cut away from them. For there are many poor and sick people who are pleasing to God, good, devout, and humble, whom poverty and bodily illness preserve in the love of God; if they were rich and raised to honors, they would quickly flow away from their purpose of holiness into the depth of vices. It is not expedient for the salvation of all to have honors and riches together with health, nor does a longer life always make a person better. Therefore almighty God, wishing to show his mercy toward those whom he has chosen, permits the good, righteous, and innocent to be subject to various calamities. And sometimes through demons, sometimes through evil people, sometimes through various other ways and means, he takes away from such people riches and honors, which he foresees they would use badly, so that they may preserve in poverty and abasement the humility which, if placed in wealth and exaltation, they would by no means have preserved. He also very often permits many great illnesses to befall them, when cheerful bodily health would have brought the greatest sickness upon the mind. Finally, he permits certain people to be driven to death by harmful magic, so that there may be cut away from them the freedom to sin which they would have abused if they had been allowed to live longer. Hence Scripture says of the righteous man: “He was taken away lest malice should change his understanding, and lest deceit should deceive his soul.”

The eighth reason for divine permission is so that human beings may venerate the sacraments of the Church, which have great power against all the harmful works of malign spirits. For one who venerates with due honor the sacraments and rites of the Catholic Church is rarely harmed by the harmful works of demons. And by the confession of witches themselves we have often heard that hearing Masses and using things blessed by the Church greatly weaken the powers of demons. For they are not blessed in the Church of God in vain, but so that they may be, as it were, little signs of divine protection, showing demons defenses to be feared. Concerning children and infants, however, who, reborn in Christ, are sometimes killed by the harmful works of demons or of human beings, we do not doubt that divine providence permits this to happen for their salvation, since it knows how to order all things for the better for mortals. Yet it often happens that infants perish by harmful magic because of the sins of their parents.

On the Providence of God, Question Eight.

Your Serenity’s eighth question was this: whether it can be proved by natural reason, as well as by the holy Scriptures, that God has care for human affairs and actions, and a certain and infallible providence over all things, both collectively and individually, that are done in the world.

I remember that I replied to this question as follows: The whole world, heaven and earth and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence, by whose will and command they were brought into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the whole...

For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us prove this opinion first by the Scriptures, and afterward confirm it by reasons, as briefly as we may.

In the Book of Judith we read: “All your ways are peaceful, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the wisest king, Solomon, speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth occasion to make your soul sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps the Lord, angered by your words, destroy all the works of your hands.” The clearest testimonies of providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel, when our Savior says to his disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them falls upon the earth before God?” Great is this commendation of divine providence, which has care not only for men but also for tiny birds. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would not believe that he has care for great ones? “Look,” he says, “at the birds of the sky, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” And a little later he adds, saying: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, O you of little faith?”

Because almighty God created all things and brought them into being when they did not exist, he rules and governs the universe, lest it slip and fall away; and this could by no means happen if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is removed, it must necessarily follow that the ordered continuity of the whole universe is thrown into confusion. But the providence of the Creator cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds, gives beasts their food, fills every animal with blessing, and clothes the grass of the field, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful grace, cannot forget man, whom he created from the beginning in his own image. He who governs all things cares for all things, and he exercises providence not only over man but also over all beasts; for all things are placed under his rule, and there is no one who can resist his will in anything.

Let us now therefore consider this vast machine of the whole universe: how it always persists in its original disposition and motion in the most orderly fashion. Unless we shamefully depart from reason, we shall understand by the clearest reasoning that that divine and unchangeable providence preserves, directs, and governs these things. Next let us contemplate all earthly things, how each and every one is born and proceeds in its natural disposition in the most orderly way. This cannot happen by chance; rather, they must be moved by the will of him by whose power they were made and created. Consequently, let us also contemplate the earth, placed in the middle of the world like a point or center, around which the whole universe unfolds at an equal distance; nothing more beautiful, nothing more adorned, nothing finally more delightful could offer itself to the senses for contemplation. In this point, enclosed by the immense mass itself, we see all things wonderfully ordered; and we see that nothing can be left unordered, so that all things which at times seem to us somehow to drift about we may know for certain not to lack, within the order of the universe, their own particular order. For by the simple and wholly unchangeable command of God, the whole machine of the entire universe, assembled out of so many different and movable things, works together and is ruled in the most orderly fashion.

We certainly see, in those things that often present themselves to our senses, that the greater the intelligence and power that arises over time in any governor, the less there [unclear] can anything disordered occur by random chance. Therefore, since that highest intellect, the creator, preserver, and ruler of all things, almighty God, rules and governs the world by his unchangeable providence, holding all things under his command, surely no place anywhere is left for rash chance, which would obstruct the will of so great a majesty.

Therefore the whole universe, whatever exists anywhere or can exist, is contained under the command of the one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. Unexpected accidents happen to us because we are changeable and are changed almost daily, having no determinate knowledge of future things. But that best maker of all things, God, since he is altogether unchangeable, knows all things, beholds all things, and understands all things together and at once. His providence is not deceived; his will is never changed; his power is not broken; his ordering is not violated; his counsel is never intercepted, even if his sentence sometimes seems to be changed. Hence, if we pay careful attention, we shall plainly understand that the ends of things and of motions...

Aut ergo deus nihil extra se intelligit vel agit, quod est falsum, aut agendo omnia et singula etiam eadem intelligit, quod est verum. Nusquam enim fierent nisi prius (ut more nostro loquamur) intelligerentur ab ipso deo, qui facit ea, sicuti non fiunt a sole, quae non prospiciuntur ab eo. Verum quia omnia et singula quae facit omnipotens intelligit, haud dubium, quin disponit regit et ordina omnia quae fecit, a quo res non solum habent ut sint, sed etiam ut causae quaedam aliarum rerum. Itaque si habent a deo res ut sint causae, inde quoque acciperunt officium causae proprium, hoc est conservare pro viribus, et curare quod fecerunt. Quo circa si a prima causa omnes causae hanc habent proprietatem, in quantum sunt quaedam causae, merito ipsa hanc bonitatem naturaliter habet ac providentiam ut omnia curet et singula quae fecit, in quantu maxime est causa coorum omnium et singulorum. Quae quidem nisi singillatim custodiantur ab eo qui facit ea, non custodientur unquam communia quae conservantur in singulis. Nec enim conservabitur totum quod ex partibus constat, si partes ipsae negliguntur. Ex intentione igitur intelligentiae priam maxima communis prouenit universales distinctio rerum. Ipsa vero per se distinguitur ab alijs, cetera; inter se suae notionis norma distinguunt. Unde sicut distinctissime deus omnia et singula novit, ita et distinctissime regit modus ratur et curat. Manifestum igitur puto clementissime Caesar Maximiliane et satis ostensum, quod providentia summi rectoris dei inferiora omnia et singula amplectitur, disponit, regit et moderatur, quae alioquin sine observantis provida dispositione hunc ordinem quem cernimus pulcherrimum nullatenus continuarent. Nec me fugit quam uarie quondam huius mundi sapientes de providentia fuerint opinati. Ex his quidam non providentia, sed casu factum hunc mundum arbitrati sunt, quorum si esset opinio uera, nullus relinqueret providentiae locus, sed necessario fluitarent omnia cum eo mundus quo factus est casu posset interire. Contra quorum falsam opinionem alij docuerunt, nec fieri mundum sine ratione potuisset, nec constare certe, nisi summa providentia factoris regeretur. Hinc Boëcius vir Christiani 62 nīssimus dixit. O qui perpetua mundum ratione gubernas. Terrarũ coelique sator, qui tempus ab eo ire iubes, stabilisque manens das cuncta mo- ueri. Iterumque dixit. Omnium generatio rerum, cunctosque mutabilium naturarum progressus, et quiequid mouetur aliquo modo, causas, ordinẽ, formas, ex diuine mentis stabilitate sortitur. Sed hi tur= piter errauerunt, quoniam omnipotens non so= lum uniuersalium et incorruptibilium, sed etid particularium et corruptibilium providen= ciam habet et curam. Unde sanctus iterum= Boëcius dicit. Sedet in terra conditor altus re= rumque regens flecit habenas, rex et dominus, fons et origo, lex, & sapiens arbiter aequi. Hic est cunctis continuus amor, repetuntque boni sine teneri, quia non aliter durare queunt, nis̄ conuerto rursus amore refluant cause quas de= dit ipse. Alijuero neglectum se iri nō ferentes, hominem propter intellectus praeminentiam de numero cor=

The lower things will declare that all these things are done, preserved, disposed, and moved by divine providence, to whose command absolutely nothing is alien. For God himself, the ruler of all things, understands both all things and each thing, not stretched out, after our manner, among many things, but abiding in himself as an indivisible one; and by beholding himself as the exemplar of the whole universe and the cause of causes, and through causes as the cause of all things, he contemplates all things, and in contemplating all things he cares and provides for them, directing each thing to its end and good in everlasting order.

Come now, most wise Caesar: in order that we may understand divine providence governing all things, let us use arguments as brief as we can for our purpose. And so, if God’s action is his own intelligence, which no wise man fails to admit, as being at once most eminent and most inward, then as much as he acts, so much surely he understands, and conversely. But he acts in each thing, not only in great things but also in the smallest; therefore he understands each thing. For the most abundant influx of the first being passes through each thing that in any way exists, following in fixed orders; and the things that act after him are everywhere moved by his power and act.

Therefore either God understands or acts nothing outside himself, which is false, or, by acting upon all things and each thing, he also understands those same things, which is true. For they would nowhere come to be unless first, to speak in our manner, they were understood by God himself, who makes them, just as those things are not made by the sun which are not looked upon by it. But since the Almighty understands all things and each thing that he makes, there is no doubt that he disposes, rules, and orders all things that he has made; from him things have not only that they exist, but also that they are certain causes of other things. And so, if things have from God that they are causes, from him too they have received the office proper to a cause, that is, to preserve according to their powers and to care for what they have made. Therefore, if all causes have this property from the first cause, insofar as they are certain causes, deservedly that cause itself naturally has this goodness and providence, so that it cares for all things and each thing that it has made, insofar as it is in the highest degree the cause of all those things, both collectively and singly. And unless these are guarded individually by him who makes them, the common things that are preserved in individuals will never be guarded. For neither will the whole that consists of parts be preserved if the parts themselves are neglected.

From the intention of the first and greatest intelligence, therefore, comes the common universal distinction of things. It itself is distinguished from others through itself; the rest it distinguishes among themselves by the standard of its own conception. Hence, just as God knows all things and each thing most distinctly, so too he most distinctly rules, moderates, and cares for them. I think it is therefore clear, most clement Caesar Maximilian, and sufficiently shown, that the providence of God, the supreme ruler, embraces, disposes, rules, and governs all lower things and each thing; otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who observes them, they would in no way continue this most beautiful order that we discern.

Nor am I unaware how variously the wise men of this world once thought about providence. Some of them judged that this world was made not by providence but by chance; if their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence, but all things would necessarily drift, and the world, since it was made by chance, could perish by chance. Against their false opinion others taught that the world could not have been made without reason, nor certainly could it stand unless it were ruled by the highest providence of its maker. Hence Boethius, a most Christian man, said: “O you who govern the world by everlasting reason, maker of earth and heaven, who command time to go forth from eternity, and, remaining stable, grant that all things be moved.” And again he said: “The generation of all things, and all the developments of changeable natures, and whatever is moved in any way, receive their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.”

Others, however, thought that God cared only for incorruptible things, such as the heavenly things and separate substances, and likewise the species of things, but that he was wholly ignorant of all the rest and utterly neglected them. But these men erred shamefully, because the Almighty has providence and care not only for universal and incorruptible things, but also for particular and corruptible things. Hence Saint Boethius again says: “The lofty founder of things sits upon the earth and, ruling, bends the reins, king and lord, fountain and origin, law, and wise judge of what is just. He is the continuous love for all things, and they seek to be held by the end of the good, because they cannot endure otherwise, unless, turned back again by love, they flow back to the causes that he himself gave.”

Others, however, unable to bear that they should be neglected, [claimed] that man, because of the preeminence of his intellect, [unclear].

36
corruptibiliũ exemerunt, dicentes deum hominis curam et providentiam habere, reliqua vero terrestria cuncta despicere. Contra quorum falsam opinionem et satis reor dictum, et multa producere omnino superfluum. Ait enim scriptura: Homines et iumenta saluabitis domine. Et in alio loco quidam sapiens dixit: Pusillum et magnum fecit dominus, et aequaliter est illi cura de omnibus. Omnia igitur et singula inferiora, magna et parua, corruptibilia et incorruptibilia divinae maiestatis prouidentia ordinat, regit, disponit et curat, cuius voluntas potentissima ex nihilom omnia produxit, sacra iterum protestante scriptura. Tua vero pater providentia ab initio cuncta gubernat. Erubescant igitur homines mente corrupti et impii ac reprobii circa fidem Christianam, qui una loquacitate inflati prouidentiam omnia scientis auserunt, et quantam deo iniuriam faciant non attendunt. Quid enim ut Firmiani utamur sententia, tam dignum tamque proprium omnipotenti deo, quam prouidentia? Sed si nihil prouidet, si inferiora negligit, si mortalia non curat, amisit iam omne 63 nem dignitatem. Sed impossibile est sancto attestante Anhelmo, deum honorem suum perdere, quoniam sicut Peripatheticus ait -in eternis non est malum, nec corruptio, nec peccatum. Qui ergo providentiam tollit, totam dei substantiam tollit, & quid dicit, nisi deum non esse? Sed dicant mihi nunc qui dei providentiam negant inferiora curare. Si deus inferiora negligt, attendant quid necessario sequatur. Si deus scienter nos negligit et contemnit, non est iam deinceps causa, qua ipsum uel cultu prosequamur uel religione ueneremur, a quo nullum assequimur beneficium, quin po- tius neglecti et contempti, negligamus et il- lum ipsi. Si uero nesciens nos contemnit ac neg- ligit, penitus iam causa non est ut nescientem nos et ob id nihil boni conferre potentem co- lamus aut precibus inuocemus. Nam si non cu- rat humana deus, sive sciens, sive nesciens, cessat omnis causa pietatis, cum sit spes nulla [unclear] Salutis. Qua nam potest inter mortales pietatis esse consideratio, qua spes animarum salutis, si deus humana non curat. Enimuero si prouidentia tollitur, quem colimus, quem adoramus? Si non est apud deum prouidentia mortalium, certe neque beneficia praestat hominibus, neque poenas desertoribus imponit, neque mortales iuare potest, nec uult nec omnino curat, nec quid agamus aduertit, & neque preces, neque orationes cuiusquam exaudit. Cur autem illi cultum exhibemus ullum, cur honorem, cur preces, aut quare nescientem nos deum tantopere metuimus uel timemus, qui nobis neglectis atque contemptis, neque benefacere potest, neque male? Prouidentia enim sublata neque sanctitas, neque religio subsiftet, quibus extinctis perturbatio uita sequetur maxima, & confusio horrenda. Pietate in deum sublata, quid iam erit respublica, nisi confusio semper terna? Peribit necessario fides hominum publica, societasque humani generis, iusticiaque omnis una simul euanescent et peribunt. Quid erit de Christiana fide sentiendum, si deus non curat humana, quid denique de saluatorc omniuna 64 vium domino nostro Iesu Christo, nisi fabula inanis, & fictitium totum reputabitur, si non est providentia dei mortalia curans. Proinde quicquid in hac uita boni agimus, quicquid pro dei amore mali sustinemus, uanum est totum ac nobis inutile, si ille de nobis curam non habet ullam. Videant nunc et horreant qui prouidentiam dei negant, cum finem opinionis suae desperationem omnium peßimam intuentur. Nemo igitur se uaniloquentia philosophorum seculariũ inductus ad contemptum dei erudiat, nemo prouidentiam summi et incommutabili boni tollat, nemo dignitatem creatoris omnium corrumpat. Omnes enim qui prouidentiam negant divinam, beneficis clementissimi saluatoris et indignos se praestant et ingratos. Firmiter enim credendũ est et nullatenus du bitandũ hũc mundũ uniuersum ta uisibilem qua inuisibilem, omniaque et singula, quae uel in caelo sunt

They exempted [man] from corruptible things, saying that God has care and providence for man, but despises all other earthly things. Against their false opinion I think enough has been said, and to bring forward many arguments would be wholly superfluous. For Scripture says: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord.” And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made the small and the great, and he has equal care for all.”

Therefore the providence of the divine majesty orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all and each of the lower things, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible; his most powerful will produced all things from nothing, as sacred Scripture again bears witness: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.”

Let men corrupt in mind, impious and reprobate concerning the Christian faith, therefore be ashamed: those who, puffed up with mere talk, have dared to deny the providence of the all-knowing one, and do not consider how great an injury they do to God. For what, to use the judgment of Firmianus, is so worthy and so proper to almighty God as providence? But if he provides for nothing, if he neglects lower things, if he does not care for mortal things, he has now lost all dignity. But it is impossible, as holy Anselm bears witness, for God to lose his honor, since, as the Peripatetic says, in eternal things there is no evil, no corruption, and no sin. Therefore whoever removes providence removes the whole substance of God; and what does he say, except that God does not exist?

But let those who deny that God’s providence cares for lower things now tell me this. If God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, there is henceforth no reason why we should honor him with worship or venerate him with religion, since we obtain no benefit from him; rather, being neglected and despised, let us ourselves neglect him too.

But if he unknowingly despises and neglects us, there is now utterly no reason why we should worship one who does not know us, and for that reason cannot confer any good, or invoke him with prayers. For if God does not care for human affairs, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every reason for piety ceases, since there is no hope [unclear] of salvation.

What regard for piety can there be among mortals, what hope for the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence is removed, whom do we worship, whom do we adore? If there is no providence for mortals with God, certainly he neither bestows benefits on men, nor imposes punishments on apostates, nor can help mortals, nor wishes to, nor cares at all, nor notices what we do, and he hears neither the prayers nor the petitions of anyone. Why then do we offer him any worship, why honor, why prayers, or why do we so greatly fear or dread a God who does not know us, who, having neglected and despised us, can do us neither good nor harm?

For when providence has been removed, neither holiness nor religion will remain; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and dreadful confusion will follow. With piety toward God removed, what will the commonwealth now be except everlasting confusion? Public trust among men will necessarily perish, and the society of the human race and all justice together with it will vanish and perish. What is to be thought of the Christian faith if God does not care for human affairs? Finally, what is to be thought of the Savior of all the living, our Lord Jesus Christ, unless the whole thing will be regarded as an empty tale and a fiction, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? Therefore whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is wholly vain and useless to us if he has no care for us at all.

Let those who deny the providence of God now see and tremble, when they behold the end of their opinion: the worst despair of all. Therefore let no one, led on by the empty talk of worldly philosophers, instruct himself in contempt of God; let no one remove the providence of the highest and unchangeable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of and ungrateful for the benefits of the most merciful Savior.

For it must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole universe, both visible and invisible, and all and each of the things that are either in heaven...

37
Sunt vel in terra, & in mari divina providentia regi et gubernari, & nihil penitus in toto universo ab eius cura alienum. Nam et fruges et reliqua omnia quae terra parit, tempestates quoque ac varietates temporum coeli et mutationes, quibus omnia quae terra gignit maturata pubescunt, divina providentia generi humano praestat, procurat et omnia et singula, nec solum magnas et minima quae, usque adeo, ut nec tenuissimum quidem arboris folium in terram decidat sine uoluntate omnipotentis dei patris, qui creavit illud et regit et curat. Si quis autem putat hanc totam universi magnitudinem ab uno deo qui solus est non posse regi et gubernari, nimium fallitur, & quanta sit virtus divinae potestatis nescire comprobatur. Enimvero qui universum mundum ex nihilo potuit in esse producere, etiam quod fecit prudentissime in sempiternum potest gubernare. Omnia enim novit, omnia inteligit, omnia potest, qui solus omnipotens omnia creavit. Nos igitur Sancto Evangelio credentes divi 65 Siuinam inprimis providentiam veneremur, mentes quoque nostras qua possumus virtute sur sum erigamus ab his qua sunt caduca, & nobis ipsis redacti uniamur, quatenus dei maiestatem ubique praesentem fideliter intelligamus, que cum sit omnino incircumscribibilis tenet om- nia, implet omnia, complectitur omnia, su- perexcedit omnia, & sustinet omnia. Non autè ex una parte sustinet, atque ex alia superex cedit, neque ex una parte implet, atque ex alia cir cumplectitur, sed circumplectendo implet, & implendo circumplectitur, sustinendo super ex cedit, et super excedendo sustinet omnia, qui per molem corporis nusquam est, & per incircum scriptibilem substantiam suam nusquam deest, qui oculis carnis non cernitur, qui per fidem in cordis puritate uidetur. O virtus inexplicabili- lis. O pietas incomprehensibilis. O sapi- entia ineffabilis. O diuinitas incircumscrip- tibilis, que non partibus constas, ut corpus, non affectibus ditas, ut anima, non formis sub stas, ut caetera omnia que per te facta sunt, que es in omnibus et super omnia, regens et gubernans sapientisime uniuersa. His itaque testimonijs sacratisime Caesar Maximilianesa tis ut reor probatum est mundum hunc univers sum dei prouidentia gubernari, qui cum fit in tellectus purus, simplex, increatus, & sempit ernus, omnia nouit, omnia intelligit, omnia percognoscit, atque omnipotens natura cum fit omnia potens potest, cui nihil est difficile, ni hil impossibile, qui tam miranda creauit poten tia sua in ueritate constituit, ratione perfecit, uirtute sustinet, bonitate illustrat, ipsi laus, ipsi honor, ipsi gloria qui uiuit et regnat de us gloriosus et excelfus in fecula feculorum Amen. AVTHORIS PRO testatio ad Caela rem. H Aec sunt Maximiliane Caesar inuictif sime, quae mihi ad Octo quaestiones et tua maiestate propositas uidebantur di cenda. Voluisti etenime arundem etiam et me habere iudicium in scriptis, supra ueritatem de 66 de me faciens estimationem, qui illis comparandus non sum ingenio, quorum ante me sententiam audiui, faciat me uenia dignum si quid minus proprium dixi, quod imperio celsitudinis tuae viator in itinere constitutus ut potui per intervalla quod respondendum occurrebat dictau. Dico autem ex mente et mani festè protestor me Christianae fidei sincerum confesscrem, et in unionc sacro sancta Romana ecclesie usque ad mortem uelle permanere. Unde si quid uel in hac lucubratione mea uel in alijs haberetur dictum uel scriptum, aliter quam illa tenet, sentit, credit et docet, ut uerus obedientiae filius, praesentium attestatione denuncio, et uolo simpliciter esse et haberi perpetuo reuocatum. Quocirca maiestatem tuam sapientissime Caesar, et humiliter rogo et instanter commonefacio, ut priusquam responsiones meas ad notitiam facias peruenire illorum quibus destinata seruantur, multorum facias iudicio comprobari. Summopere namque curandum est, ut nihil proponatur illis qui bus tua serenitas ad salutem inuigilat, nisi solidum, probatum, manifestum, et sententia plurimorum sapientum in fide catholica legi time confirmatum. Omnipotens deus te sua prouidentia dirigat et custodiat semper, ad laudem nominis sui Maximiliane imperato rum maxime. Ex ciuitate Neometans, decima die mensis Iulij. Anno Christianoru Mil lesimo quingentesi mo Octauo. Ioannes Tritemius Abbas. IMPRES- SVM FR ANCO FORTI PER CY- RIACVM IA COBVM. Anno. 1550. IMPRESE IN MANV CORREGIS DOMINI.

Whether on earth or in the sea, they are ruled and governed by divine providence, and nothing at all in the whole universe is outside his care. For divine providence provides for the human race the crops and all the other things the earth brings forth, and also storms, the varieties of the seasons, and the changes of the sky, by which all things that the earth produces ripen and mature. It takes care of all things and each thing, not only the great but also the very smallest, to such a degree that not even the thinnest leaf of a tree falls to the earth without the will of almighty God the Father, who created it and rules and cares for it. But if anyone thinks that this whole vastness of the universe cannot be ruled and governed by one God, who alone is God, he is greatly mistaken, and is shown not to know how great the power of divine might is. Indeed, he who was able to bring the whole world from nothing into being can also most wisely govern forever what he made. For he knows all things, understands all things, can do all things, who alone, being omnipotent, created all things.

Therefore we, believing the holy Gospel, let us above all venerate divine providence, and let us also raise our minds upward, with what strength we can, away from these things that are perishable; and, brought back to ourselves, let us be united, so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God present everywhere. Since it is wholly uncircumscribable, it holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. It does not sustain from one part and surpass from another, nor fill from one part and encompass from another; but by encompassing it fills, and by filling it encompasses; by sustaining it surpasses, and by surpassing it sustains all things. By bodily mass he is nowhere, and by his uncircumscribable substance he is nowhere absent; he is not perceived by the eyes of flesh, but is seen through faith in purity of heart.

O inexplicable power. O incomprehensible loving-kindness. O ineffable wisdom. O uncircumscribable divinity, which is not composed of parts, as a body is; is not enriched by affections, as a soul is; does not underlie forms, as do all the other things that have been made through you; which is in all things and above all things, most wisely ruling and governing the universe.

By these most sacred testimonies, therefore, most sacred Caesar Maximilian, I think it has been sufficiently proved that this whole world is governed by God’s providence. Since he is pure understanding, simple, uncreated, and eternal, he knows all things, understands all things, and fully comprehends all things; and since he is omnipotent by nature, being able to do all things, he can do all things. For him nothing is difficult, nothing impossible. He created such wondrous things by his power, established them in truth, perfected them by reason, sustains them by might, and illuminates them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory, who lives and reigns, God glorious and exalted, forever and ever. Amen.

The author’s protestation to Caesar.

These, most invincible Caesar Maximilian, are the things that seemed to me should be said in reply to the eight questions proposed by your majesty. For you wished to have my judgment also on the same matters in writing, making an estimate of me beyond the truth. I am not to be compared in talent with those whose opinion I heard before my own. Let pardon make me worthy if I have said anything less suitable, since at the command of your highness, being a traveler set upon the road, I dictated as I could, at intervals, whatever occurred to me as needing answer.

I say, however, from my heart and openly protest that I am a sincere confessor of the Christian faith, and that I wish to remain until death in the union of the most holy Roman Church. Therefore if anything, either in this little work of mine or in others, should be found said or written otherwise than that Church holds, thinks, believes, and teaches, I, as a true son of obedience, by the attestation of these presents declare and wish it simply to be, and to be held forever, revoked.

For this reason, most wise Caesar, I humbly beg and earnestly admonish your majesty that, before you cause my responses to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are being kept, you have them approved by the judgment of many. For the greatest care must be taken that nothing be proposed to those over whose salvation your serenity keeps watch unless it is solid, approved, manifest, and lawfully confirmed in the Catholic faith by the opinion of very many wise men.

May almighty God direct and preserve you always by his providence, to the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors. From the city of Neometum, on the tenth day of the month of July, in the year of Christians one thousand five hundred and eight.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot.
